bullets: CXBench is a new benchmark that scores both the final result and the procedure followed by tool-using customer-service agents across six regulated domains. Its rule cards connect regulatory obligations to observable trace evidence, so an agent cannot receive full credit merely by reaching the right business state while skipping disclosures, consent, or required steps. Why it matters: If you evaluate agents for regulated workflows, CXBench changes the acceptance decision from “did it finish?” to “did it finish through an auditable, compliant process?” This can expose systems whose outcome scores hide deployment-blocking behavior. Evidence: E011. High confidence.

VibeTraining-Bench is a new benchmark for research agents that iteratively improve an entire agent system under a fixed resource budget. Agents use validation feedback to modify training data, the trainer, and the inference harness—the software that controls how a model receives prompts, uses tools, and produces answers—before selecting a final system. Why it matters: If you are comparing agents for automated model development, this evaluates cross-component engineering rather than isolated task solving. It can distinguish an agent that improves one component locally from one that allocates a limited budget across interacting data, training, and inference choices. Evidence: E002. High confidence.

HoloCosm is a new method for compressing benchmarks while preserving several evaluation metrics at once. Its authors report that at 80% compression, five methods selecting samples for one metric produced more cross-metric reconstruction error than equal-size random sampling in over 70% of comparisons. Why it matters: If you reduce a test suite to control evaluation cost, selecting examples to preserve one score may distort other scores and model rankings. HoloCosm makes multi-metric preservation part of the subset-selection decision rather than assuming one representative metric is enough. Evidence: E041. High confidence.

Goal Images Are Control Targets reports that general image-editing quality did not predict robotic usefulness. Across two goal-conditioned manipulation policies, highly ranked image editors produced worse control targets than smaller fine-tuned open models, with a larger gap on multi-step tasks. Why it matters: If you are choosing an image generator to guide a robot toward a desired scene, image-quality leaderboards are not sufficient evidence. The relevant selection test is whether generated images improve downstream control, because visually strong edits can still encode unsuitable spatial targets. Evidence: E034. High confidence.

LEAPS is a new long-context benchmark that separates three abilities: recalling a fact already present, tracking a state through a sequence of transformations, and learning a pattern from many observations to make a prediction. Its authors position this against existing tests that primarily measure recall. Why it matters: If you are selecting a long-context model for agents with lengthy histories, a recall-heavy score may not show whether the model can maintain changing task state or infer recurring behavior. LEAPS provides a way to test those capabilities separately instead of treating context length as one ability. Evidence: E004. High confidence.

SWE-Residual is a new coding-agent benchmark for starting-state robustness: maintaining performance when a repository already contains earlier work reported as complete but still has incorrect or missing pieces. Standard software-engineering benchmarks generally begin from a clean state. Why it matters: If you are choosing agents to continue human or agent-written code, clean-start results may not represent the actual handoff. This benchmark tests whether an agent can identify residual defects without an explicit description of what remains wrong. Evidence: E023. High confidence.
briefing.caveat: This is a keyword-filtered feed, not a representative sample of artificial intelligence research. The briefing received 177 selected evidence records from a 755-record corpus, so it did not review every captured artifact. Brave and OpenReview were unavailable, and several attention collectors reported unread or stale carry-forward records; no attention metric is used in these findings.

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating LLMs for crisis communication requires more than judging isolated responses, because public feedback and competitor actions can reshape trust over time. Existing benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, offering limited evidence about long-horizon risk-sensitive communication. We introduce \textbf{BrandEval}, a two-track benchmark for product-crisis communication, focusing on public brand responses to product-related safety, quality, service, and trust incidents. BrandEval-Static evaluates stakeholder-aware strategic analysis, while BrandEval-Dynamic stress-tests response policies in \textbf{BrandPolis}, a controlled multi-agent sandbox with consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust-risk trajectories. We also construct \textbf{BrandSRD}, a Chinese crisis-response dataset, and instantiate a reference Strategic Agent using \textbf{Strategic Rationale (SR)}. Across proprietary and open-source models, we find that static strategic quality is informative but incomplete: it aligns with some end-state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility and delayed recovery; dynamic stress tests further expose tail-risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/BrandEval.
evidence_items.title: BrandEval: A Two-Track Multi-Agent Benchmark for Risk-Sensitive LLM Crisis Communication

evidence_items.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTrainingBench.
evidence_items.title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement

It encompasses two primary types of tasks:1. Data-oriented tasks: including data-retrieval, data-analysis, data-management, and data-processing problems.2. Computation-oriented tasks: including simulation problems, and specialized models and toolkits problems. Contents - questions and answers/: the benchmark with questions and ground-truth answers (keys: user query, sources, input type, output type, answer, absolute tolerance, unit, solution code or process, reference link, official documentation, notes), with a verified reference implementation per question in the corresponding solution code/ directories.- The archive also includes the per-task result records (results/), a script that recomputes the paper's benchmark results (scoring/), and the evaluated framework and model versions (EVALUATIONS.md). Access This archive is password-protected to prevent data contamination. The password can be found in the benchmark tasks and results/README.md of the associated GitHub repository (https://github.com/CederGroupHub/CASCADE). Please DO NOT redistribute the unzipped data files or related data online.

evidence_items.summary: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.
evidence_items.title: LEAPS: Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern Learning and State Tracking

evidence_items.summary: Prompt injection is the dominant security risk for large-language-model (LLM) applications and agents, yet the field still lacks a coherent map of how these attacks are constructed. More than twenty public datasets describe prompt injection using incompatible vocabularies, often organized around delivery vector, attacker goal, or generation method. In this Systematization of Knowledge, we present PIAtlas, a taxonomy organized instead around how the injected instruction is constructed to subvert the underlying model. Its six classes, one per subversion mechanism, form the roots of a hierarchy of techniques and sub-techniques that researchers can use to describe attacks consistently and design more systematic evaluations. We derive the taxonomy from how LLMs are trained, prompted, and influenced by human-like framing, and compare it with historical attack data. To ground this comparison, we release PICorpus, to our knowledge the largest license-clean collection of public prompt-injection datasets, and map thousands of its records to PIAtlas under a human-verified protocol. The mapping shows that attacks usually combine several techniques drawn from only a few mechanisms. It also reveals gaps that existing labels obscure: widely used agent benchmarks test only part of the attack space, and adaptive attackers favor mechanisms that curated benchmarks underrepresent. PIAtlas thus provides a common foundation for understanding this attack space, improving benchmark coverage, and guiding red teaming and defenses.
evidence_items.title: SoK: PIAtlas: Decomposing the Unbounded Prompt Injection Attack Space

evidence_items.summary: While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. Recent evaluations on benchmarks like HybridDeepResearch show that even frontier agents struggle when evidence must cross this boundary. While these benchmarks have exposed the limitation, methodologies to explicitly teach cross-source reasoning remain absent. To address this, we introduce HybridResearcher, a 4B agent trained to bridge evidence across the structured and unstructured boundary. To build it, we synthesize cross-source bridge trajectories by starting with validated single-source tasks-such as existing text-to-SQL or web search queries-and fabricating the missing source around a bridge entity drawn from the seed's own output. We retain a sample only when strict construction gates confirm that neither side alone suffices, ensuring the data requires true cross-source interdependence. Finally, we train on this curated dataset using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Evaluated on the existing HybridDeepResearch benchmark, HybridResearcher improves over our base model, Qwen3.5-4B, by 30.0 points pass@8 and surpasses the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B by 8.3 points, while also improving over its base model on established, held-out single-source benchmarks (BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus), demonstrating that this complex cross-source reasoning can be taught directly to small models without triggering catastrophic forgetting.
evidence_items.title: HybridResearcher: Bridging the Structured-Unstructured Boundary for Deep Research Agents

evidence_items.summary: The proposed road-surface dataset was developed for automated road-surface condition assessment, road-damage classification, and computer vision applications for infrastructure monitoring. It contains three classes: Major Damage, Minor Damage, and Normal, representing different levels of road-surface conditions. The images were collected in Barishal district, Bangladesh, under natural road and weather conditions. They capture diverse surface textures, lighting conditions, viewpoints, and road surroundings. Each image was visually inspected and labeled according to the dominant road-surface condition. Major Damage includes severe potholes, significant cracks, deformation, and extensive surface loss. Minor Damage contains small holes, local cracks, surface imperfections, and minor deformations. Normal represents road surfaces without significant visible damage. The dataset contains 2,855 original images, comprising 1,907 Major Damage, 354 Minor Damage, and 594 Normal images. Before augmentation, the images were split into training, validation, and test sets in a 7:1:2 ratio, resulting in 1,996, 290, and 569 images, respectively. Splitting was performed before augmentation to prevent data leakage across subsets. To address class imbalance, 2,504 additional training images were generated using random rotation, brightness and contrast adjustment, Gaussian blurring, and hue and saturation shifts. These included 166 Major Damage, 1,253 Minor Damage, and 1,085 Normal images. Consequently, the final training set contains 4,500 balanced images, with 1,500 images per class, comprising 1,996 original and 2,504 augmented images. The dataset contains 5,359 unique original and augmented images across all subsets. Images were standardized to 1024 × 1024 pixels while preserving their original aspect ratios through black padding where necessary, avoiding geometric distortion of road features. For model training and evaluation, images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels.
evidence_items.title: PavementSense: A benchmark dataset for road surface damage severity classification

evidence_items.summary: "This dataset collection brings together benchmark datasets for multivariate time series analysis, supporting four major tasks: forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification. It covers diverse application domains and temporal characteristics, including heterogeneous variable distributions, periodic patterns, long-term trends, abrupt changes, and anomalous behaviors.The collection includes established public benchmarks, such as ETT, Electricity, Weather, Exchange Rate, MSL, SMAP, PSM, SMD, SWaT, and datasets from the UEA Time Series Classification Archive. The availability of individual datasets depends on their original distribution terms and access requirements.The purpose of this collection is to facilitate systematic evaluation and reproducible research on multivariate time series analysis. Dataset-specific descriptions, source references, file organization, preprocessing procedures, and usage instructions are provided in the accompanying documentation. Users should consult the original sources for dataset-specific conditions and cite the original datasets appropriately when using them in research.This collection provides a practical benchmark resource for researchers developing and evaluating unified time series analysis methods across multiple tasks."
evidence_items.title: "A Benchmark Dataset Collection for Multivariate Time Series Analysis"

evidence_items.summary: AI systems may miss indirect, culturally situated distress or provide support mismatched to the application context. Existing benchmarks do not jointly address cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. We introduce VEILED-SH, a benchmark and construction methodology for evaluating single-turn responses to indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress. Its 10,003 prompts span counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage, drawing on Singapore-grounded sources and public datasets. An expert-validated multi-label taxonomy distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated to three peer-support practitioners and three clinicians, retain separate reference policies for proxy-alignment scoring. Evaluating five systems on a coverage-enriched sample reveals variation in proxy alignment across profile-generated reference policies, even for the same system responses.
evidence_items.title: VEILED-SH: Vulnerability Expression through Indirect Language Evaluation Dataset (Self-Harm)

evidence_items.summary: Performing accurate protein-glycan docking is critical to understanding protein-glycan interactions which govern many biological processes. However, this important task is hampered by the lack of tailored datasets, benchmarks and models for protein-glycan docking. To fill this blank, we first curate a standard benchmark ProtGlycanDock for training and evaluating protein-glycan docking models under both protein and glycan generalization settings. On this benchmark, we evaluate ten models in three categories, physics-based docking methods, machine-learning-based docking models and molecular structure prediction models. To obtain more precise binding poses, we further propose two finetuning techniques to inject the knowledge of glycan conformations into a general-purpose molecular structure prediction model. These two techniques respectively augment model inputs with glycan topological features and refine glycan binding pose with a glycan energy loss. Benchmark results show the superiority of AlphaFold 3 among existing methods, and the two proposed finetuning techniques can be well combined to achieve a state-of-the-art model for protein-glycan docking. Also, we perform stratified benchmark analysis and case studies to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of current models, providing insights for future model improvements. We maintain datasets at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ProtGlycanDock/ProtGlycanDock and source codes at https://github.com/kasawa1234/ProtGlycanDock
evidence_items.title: ProtGlycanDock: Towards Accurate Protein-Glycan Docking with Tailored Dataset, Benchmark and Model

evidence_items.summary: Tool-using language agents increasingly perform regulated customer-service workflows, where a correct final state is insufficient: agents must also provide disclosures, obtain consent, and follow required procedures. Existing tool-agent benchmarks largely score final business states, accepting trajectories that reach correct outcomes through non-compliant processes. We introduce cxbench, a benchmark that evaluates outcome and process compliance separately across six regulated domains. Each task combines a customer request, a tool-based environment, and explicit process requirements. Rule cards link cited regulatory obligations to observable trace evidence. A hybrid grader combines deterministic checks for ordering and authority with an LLM judge for semantic requirements. We define a false-pass as an outcome-pass run that fails process checks. Across seven models and 120 tasks, 55.5% of the 840 retained executions are false-passes, representing 80.1% of outcome-passing runs; only 13.8% pass both checks. Process-inclusive evaluation changes the observed model ordering and exposes differences hidden by outcome-only scoring. cxbench makes these failures inspectable through trace-linked criteria.
evidence_items.title: CXBench: A Benchmark for Process-Compliant LLM Agents in Regulated Customer-Experience Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Conversational large language models can respond with warmth and reassurance while failing to advance the user's stated goal. We conceptualize this failure as $\textbf{goal displacement}$, the substitution of persona-maintenance content for goal-relevant substance. To measure it, we introduce $\textbf{GDB}$ (Goal Displacement Benchmark), comprising 230 scenarios across nine domains and $4{,}134$ human-scored responses from 18 models. A $2 \times 2$ taxonomy crosses hard constraints with emotional distress, distinguishing failures to confront infeasible goals or combine empathy with practical guidance from reverse displacement, where unsolicited problem-solving replaces requested emotional support. A deletion-test rubric assesses whether substantive help remains after purely supportive sentences are removed. Independent raters achieve weighted $κ= 0.82$ against author scores for displacement severity. Trap displacement ranges from $0.0\%$ to $37.7\%$ and is strongly negatively correlated with Chatbot Arena Elo ($ρ= -0.706$, $n = 15$). Reverse displacement reaches $41.9\%$, including substantial rates in models with negligible trap displacement. A factorial probe supports a distinction from social sycophancy. Human-scored responses in the high-complexity, low-pressure condition exhibit $35.0\%$ sycophancy but $7.5\%$ displacement, with little association between the constructs. Matched OLMo-2 checkpoints show that mixed empathy-with-constraints displacement remains at $52.3\%$ after supervised fine-tuning and falls to $13.8\%$ after direct preference optimization. GDB provides a reproducible diagnostic of whether responses advance the operationalized user goal, supporting model comparison, post-training evaluation, and regression testing. We release the dataset, annotations, and rubric under CC-BY-4.0 and the evaluation code under MIT.
evidence_items.title: When Empathy Misses the Goal: A Benchmark for Goal Displacement in LLM Advice

evidence_items.summary: We test whether Javo, a sales agent fine-tuned on 4.6 million consented, de-identified commercial conversations, sells better than a frontier general-purpose model and better than human sales associates. The evaluation has four parts. Study 1 scores the agent on two public sales benchmarks, SalesLLM and SmartSalesBench, against 10 frontier and open-weight models. Study 2 is a randomized controlled trial on 100 live websites in 14 industries (e-commerce, travel and hospitality, and high-consideration services), run from 1 May to 30 September 2026, in which 14.8 million visitors were randomized to no agent, Javo, or a frontier-model agent with an identical interface, catalog tools and guardrails. Study 3 isolates the effect of the model by comparing those two agent arms. Study 4 compares Javo with each site's own human associates on 20 sites with staffed live chat. Relative to no agent, Javo changed revenue per visitor by +10.0% (95% CI +5.1 to +14.9). Among engaged visitors, it changed conversion by +21.6% relative to the frontier-model agent (95% CI +16.9 to +26.3). Against human associates, its engaged conversion was 11.26% versus 11.20% (non-inferior, margin -7%, one-sided p = 0.004; no significant superiority), at 1.8% of the cost per conversation. Return rates, unsupported product claims and complaint rates met the prespecified safety guardrails.
evidence_items.title: Selling in the Wild: Benchmark and Randomized Field Evidence for a Sales Agent Trained on Commercial Conversations

evidence_items.summary: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.
evidence_items.title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data

evidence_items.summary: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. GreenNIDS connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a reusable analysis dataset. Model implementations write a common set of outputs, which are ingested into a run-level table with companion tables for model configuration, feature importance, and training history. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.
evidence_items.title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments

evidence_items.summary: Reliable radio-based indoor localization is essential for industrial automation, yet existing methods are often evaluated in environments that do not fully reflect the severe multipath and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions encountered in real deployments. This limits our understanding of how AI, i.e., modern geometric, unsupervised, and semi-supervised localization methods generalize to industrial 5G settings. We present RAIL-5G, a public real-world 5G NR channel impulse response (CIR) benchmark recorded in an operational railway maintenance facility. RAIL-5G covers an 811m$^2$ indoor area with eight distributed radio units, robot-mounted user equipment (UE) trajectories, high-accuracy iGPS reference positions, and severe metal-induced multipath caused by train compartments and maintenance infrastructure. We benchmark geometric time-difference of arrival (TDoA), supervised fingerprinting, unsupervised channel charting, and self-supervised wireless pretraining methods. Our results highlight the difficulty of RAIL-5G: on the full dataset, TDoA reaches 7.02m mean average error (MAE), the best unsupervised method reaches 2.46m, and supervised fingerprinting achieves 0.52m. Self-supervised pretraining reduces the labeling effort by up to one order of magnitude, but the remaining gap to supervised learning shows that robust AI-based localization under severe multipath remains an open challenge. The dataset and code are available at https://iis.fraunhofer.de/rail-5g.
evidence_items.title: RAIL-5G: A Challenging Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for AI-Based 5G Indoor Localization

evidence_items.summary: Despite advancements in visible-thermal face recognition, where thermal probe (query) face images are matched against visible enrollment templates, existing benchmarks are currently limited by small gallery sizes (N $\approx$ 100 subjects). This limitation inhibits the ability to accurately evaluate visible-thermal facial recognition at scale and to report significant recognition performance metrics, which have better operational relevance. Therefore, we introduce VTF900, a large-scale visible-thermal face recognition benchmark with 900 subjects and paired imagery that includes expression, pose, and occlusion variations. VTF900 is designed to support large-scale (i.e., large gallery) evaluations across verification (1:1 matching) and closed-set identification (1:N matching) for visible-thermal face recognition. Furthermore, VTF900 specifically addresses the challenging combination of cross-spectral and cross-dataset analysis. In this paper, after training models on the ARL-VTF dataset, we provide benchmark analyses across convolutional (baseline), vision transformers, and domain-adaptive neural network architectures to assess how these methods scale. At full gallery scale (N = 900), transformer models achieve strong discriminative performance under frontal conditions (e.g., ViT-B: 97.68% AUC, 51.10% TAR@1%FAR), while domain-adaptive methods such as DPIT-ResNet50 demonstrate greater robustness under off-pose conditions (94.68%AUC, 36.08% TAR@1%FAR). Our results show that high AUC at small scale does not translate to reliable performance at deployment scale, and that pose variation significantly amplifies performance degradation. VTF900 exposes these limitations, enabling more rigorous evaluation of cross-spectral face recognition systems.
evidence_items.title: VTF900: A 900-Subject Visible-Thermal Face Recognition Dataset and Benchmark

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Evaluating software agents on a full benchmark is expensive. A small task subset can preserve agent rankings while yielding inaccurate scores. Historical responses provide useful structure, but tasks with identical source responses can have different outcomes for a new target agent. We introduce Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), which combines source-fitted response factors with uncertain group success rates. Observed target outcomes update the posteriors over the target latent state and group rates; posterior-guided acquisition selects subsequent tasks. Its score-based criterion equals the expected one-step reduction in full-score posterior variance. Observed successes and posterior-predictive counts for unqueried tasks yield a full-score posterior. The final estimate uses its median with source-selected calibration. At a 10% task budget on four task banks from the SWE-bench family, HSPR achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on three banks and the lowest maximum absolute error (MaxErr) on all four among the methods compared. Removing group uncertainty or replacing adaptive queries increases macro MAE in the respective controls. Macro MAE decreases across 5-20% budgets.
evidence_items.title: HSPR: Recovering Software-Agent Benchmark Scores via Hierarchical Posterior Inference

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Public leaderboards and pricing catalogues offer complementary but hard-to-combine views of the large language model ecosystem. We analyse three linked public sources: an archived Open LLM Leaderboard v2 sample of 4,565 open-weight evaluation records with complete six-benchmark scores; an 89-snapshot human-preference panel of 279 models (June 2024–August 2025); and 2,685 priced chat endpoints (October 2026). Principal component analysis identifies a dominant common component (74% of benchmark variance), retained by parallel analysis and robust to family deduplication. Benchmark performance rises with parameter count (13.6 points per tenfold) and with submission date at constant size and type (10.5 points per year) under family-clustered inference. A documented change of the default rating on 20 May 2025 shifted all listed scores by about 18 points; within the stable period the preference frontier rose by about 187 points per year relative to a fixed reference set through 17 leaders with median spells of 12 days, top-20 slots concentrated among fewer organisations, and ratings did not drift within models. Among 201 models listed by three or more providers, the median maximum-to-minimum price ratio is 1.38 (1.27 under version-strict identifiers). A hedonic model adjusting for time since first listing attributes multipliers of about 3.1 to one standard deviation of arena score and 0.18 to open-weight status, robust to version-exact matching. Preference ratings and benchmark averages agree strongly for 69 matched models. Temporal mismatch, selective coverage, and related model families preclude causal interpretation.
evidence_items.title: Capability, ranking dynamics, and inference pricing in the large language model ecosystem: evidence from linked public data

authors: Zhaoxi Zhang, Hao Liang, Linxuan Wu, Yiming Wu, Yifu Yuan, Kun Liang, Chenming Tang, Meiyi Qiang, Wentao Zhang, Weikang Li
evidence_items.summary: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.
evidence_items.title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now trade real capital using news as evidence, yet they cannot reliably tell fabricated headlines from real news. Because they read the same feeds under near-identical policies, a single fabricated post can push them into the same trade at the same moment. We present a systematic attack benchmark for information injection against LLM trading agents. Unlike prompt injection, which targets the model's instructions, information injection targets the evidence the agent trusts. The benchmark spans five injection vectors and seven event categories, evaluated over ~10,000 decisions on 15 U.S. stocks. Five findings emerge. (i) Prompt injection achieves 14% attack success rate (ASR), but fabricated news reaches 62% and two 30-word templates reach 100% on all 15 stocks, inverting the usual LLM-security intuition. (ii) For fact-poisoning templates, surface form matters more than content, since removing credibility cues such as a named source or a "BREAKING" tag drops ASR from 100% to 0% while the fake claim remains identical. (iii) Success depends on the agent's state, with a fake indicator panel scoring 91% against an agent about to hold but 12% against one about to buy. (iv) Attacks generalize across model vendors and remain effective when blended, unlabeled, into real news feeds. (v) Most attacks evade standard defenses, since model scaling stops shallow vectors but not fact poisoning, peer debate fails, and only hierarchical aggregation reduces ASR.
evidence_items.title: Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents

evidence_items.summary: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.
evidence_items.title: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents

authors: Jinze Li, Weijie Liu, Jinfeng Xu, Shuo Yang, Xin Yang, Yang Zhang, Yijin Wang, Zifei Shan, Edith C. H. Ngai
evidence_items.summary: Software engineering (SWE) benchmarks are the primary way to measure the capabilities of coding agents: an agent is placed in a code repository or machine environment, given a request, and judged by hidden tests. These benchmarks almost always start the agent from a clean state that contains no earlier work on the task. In practice, however, agents often continue work that a developer or another agent has already done and reported as complete, with no indication of what remains incorrect or missing. We introduce SWE-Residual, a benchmark for Starting-State Robustness: the ability to maintain performance on a task when the starting state already contains earlier work on that task. SWE-Residual contains 198 Residual States drawn from 111 tasks in DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench, where the earlier work modifies a code repository or a whole machine environment. Each Residual State is the state a predecessor agent left behind after submitting its work as complete, although the hidden tests still fail. The evaluated agent receives only the original request and this state, without the predecessor's trajectory or any sign that the attempt failed; because the request and hidden tests are unchanged, the starting state is the only difference from the source benchmark. Across five frontier agents, success drops by 20.6--53.5 percentage points on DeepSWE and 20.6--34.9 points on Terminal-Bench relative to a Clean Start, and agent rankings on DeepSWE reverse. Failed continuations show a pattern we call acceptance bias: agents treat the inherited work as the definition of what remains to be done instead of checking it against the request. On DeepSWE, in 58.9--88.2% of failed runs, they submit with exactly the same tests failing, although they pass most of these tests from a Clean Start. SWE-Residual thus exposes a capability gap that clean-start evaluation does not capture.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Residual: Evaluating Starting-State Robustness of Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding-based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding-based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.
evidence_items.title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures

evidence_items.summary: This reproducibility release accompanies the revised manuscript, Benchmark Integrity in Three COVID-19 and Mpox Misinformation Datasets: Duplicate Overlap, Cross-Dataset Contamination and Exploratory Label-Quality Signals. The archive provides Python implementations and analytical outputs for evaluating exact and near-duplicate content, evaluation-partition overlap, cross-corpus textual contamination, cross-dataset classification transfer, repeated-seed cross-validation and exploratory out-of-fold label-quality indicators across COVID-19-FNIR, Constraint and an mpox veracity-based analytic subset. The revised release includes five-seed model evaluation, bootstrap uncertainty estimation and a 2,000-replicate group-aware bootstrap analysis that accounts for observations sharing identical normalised texts. The archive also contains saved predictions, machine-readable statistical results, figure files, software requirements and instructions for reproducing the analyses. Original third-party datasets are not redistributed. Data-source information and input-file checksums are provided to support independent verification.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing; however, their direct application to food safety remains limited by insufficient domain knowledge, inadequate reasoning over regulatory documents, and the tendency to generate factual hallucinations. To address these challenges, this study proposes FSLLM, a domain-specific LLM designed for food safety applications. A high-quality domain corpus was constructed from diverse sources, including food safety incidents, regulatory documents, inspection reports, and industry-related materials. It initially comprised approximately 150 million tokens, of which 45,024 documents and approximately 121 million tokens were retained after decontamination. Based on the Qwen3-8B foundation model, FSLLM was developed through a two-stage training framework consisting of continual pre-training for domain knowledge adaptation and supervised fine-tuning for task alignment. Furthermore, a comprehensive benchmark covering 10 representative food safety tasks, including named entity recognition, text classification, text generation, factual verification, regulatory compliance analysis, and public health question answering, was established for systematic evaluation. Experimental results show that FSLLM outperforms the base model across multiple food safety tasks. Specifically, FSLLM achieved a Micro-F1 score of 0.5286 in named entity recognition and an accuracy of 85.21% in food safety event classification, demonstrating improvements over the base model. These findings indicate that domain-specific corpus and continual pre-training with fine-tuning enhance LLM expertise and reasoning, offering a viable solution for intelligent food safety supervision and risk analysis.
evidence_items.title: Data Engineering and Large Language Model Construction for the Food Safety Domain

evidence_items.summary: Forecasting the seasonal dynamics of Aedes albopictus, a highly invasive arbovirus vector now established across much of Europe, is a growing public health priority. Numerous mechanistic and correlative models have been developed over the last two decades, but largely in isolation, each calibrated and validated against its own data, which has prevented any assessment of where predictive capacity is genuinely limited. Rather than ranking models, which were built for different purposes and cannot be reduced to a single skill score, we establish common ground: a shared evaluation framework in which six mechanistic models, one correlative machine learning model, and two naive baseline predictors are driven by identical ERA5-Land forcing and assessed against the harmonised VectAbundance ovitrap dataset (Albania, Italy, Switzerland) using a single protocol, with robustness quantified by bootstrap resampling. We additionally combine the models into a weighted ensemble via approximate Bayesian computation. Both naive baselines outperformed every process-based and machine learning model, and the ensemble matched but did not exceed the best individual models. Predictive skill varied markedly in space, with all model classes, including the uncalibrated baselines, performing best in intensively monitored regions and worst at sparsely sampled sites. This pattern suggests that geographic variation in skill reflects the density and consistency of surveillance data more than differences in model complexity. We present this benchmark not as a league table but as shared infrastructure, common evaluation data, covariates, and protocol, on which comparable, policy-relevant forecasting tools can be built, and we argue that sustained, harmonised surveillance is the principal precondition for operational Ae. albopictus prediction.
evidence_items.title: A common benchmark for Aedes albopictus phenological models reveals surveillance data, not model complexity, as the limiting factor

evidence_items.summary: Chinese short-form dramas (duanju) drive a growing demand for automated Japanese dubbing that preserves each character’s voice. The decisive component is zero-shot cross-lingual voice cloning: synthesising Japanese speech from a short Chinese reference clip. We benchmark four neural text-to-speech systems—GPT-SoVITS v3, F5-TTS, CosyVoice2-0.5B, and the non-cloning commercial baseline EdgeTTS—on an annotated short-drama corpus (79 episodes, 3692 segments, 12 speakers) with native-speaker-verified Japanese references, combining automatic intelligibility (Whisper re-transcription) and speaker-embedding similarity with a blind listening study by five JLPT-N1 raters. Among cloning systems, only GPT-SoVITS attains usable intelligibility (character error rate 0.215, against 1.152 for F5-TTS and 4.603 for CosyVoice2), while EdgeTTS is most intelligible overall (0.030). Critically, the automatic and perceptual measures dissociate: F5-TTS scores marginally higher on embedding similarity (0.729 vs. 0.722), yet raters preferr GPT-SoVITS three to one. Naturalness shows no detectable gap between GPT-SoVITS and EdgeTTS (mean opinion score 3.08 versus 3.12, p=0.93), a null result at a resolution of about 0.6 points. In a single-speaker probe, speaker similarity rises from 0.64 to 0.71 as the reference lengthens from 3 to 10 s. Embedding similarity alone is therefore an unreliable proxy for perceived speaker identity.
evidence_items.title: Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Japanese Voice Cloning to Dub Chinese Short Dramas: A Four-System Benchmark with Human Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: The Chinese idiom "kou mi fu jian" ("honeyed words, hidden daggers") names speech that is polite in form but hostile in function. We present ZhenhuanBench, a 1,592-item benchmark built from expert commentary on Empresses in the Palace, covering speaker intent, emotion-language mismatch, and per-listener uptake. Text-only evaluation covers 34 LLMs. GPT-6 Astra leads the leaderboard at 73.48% overall, while its listener-reaction score is 58.37%. The annotations also supply supervised traces and string-verifiable training rewards. With 338 gold traces, an 8B model outperforms teacher distillation on identical items. Subsequent RL saturates, and chance correction reduces the estimated recoverable performance gap by a factor of 7.5. Our CPR-GRPO loop (Compress-Probe-Replenish) uses this estimate to weight gold supervision, reaching 67.0 on public multiple-choice tasks and 74.5 under the training-matched hidden protocol. Without target-task training, CPR outperforms Base, SFT, and GRPO across six Chinese and English pragmatic and sarcasm evaluations. On three external datasets, training with CPR yields higher mean Macro-F1 than SFT and GRPO.
evidence_items.title: Honeyed Words, Hidden Daggers: Benchmarking and Training LLMs to See Through Mock Politeness

rationale: Matched: benchmark, corpus, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs while preserving technical content and document structure and maintaining source traceability. Through continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages, we show that combining our synthetic corpus with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline. Additional experiments show how data volume, script coverage, and Indic training share affect English performance. We also introduce the Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, a multilingual benchmark suite for evaluating Indic language models across chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation. The suite combines existing Indic benchmarks with task-aware translations of English benchmarks, using automated quality assessment, targeted correction, and native-speaker review in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. We use the suite to comprehensively benchmark contemporary open-weight Indic and multilingual models across capabilities and languages, revealing substantial variation across tasks and languages. Together, these resources provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating more capable Indic language models.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Financial communication connects numerical accounts of economic activity with explanations of performance, responsibility and future expectations. Arabic financial natural language processing offers methods for studying these connections across corporate reports, market disclosures, journalism and banking interactions. Its contribution to digital humanities depends on retaining the relationship between a computational representation and the document from which it was made. This chapter follows that relationship from source collection and Arabic text processing to the analysis of vocabulary, evaluation, entities, causal attribution and multilingual reporting. It then examines what financial summaries and retrieval-grounded answers preserve or lose, and how dialectal intent detection changes the perspective from institutions speaking to institutions listening. Published Arabic resources are discussed in relation to the questions they were designed to answer, with a distinction between financial pretraining corpora, annotated datasets and evaluation benchmarks. A running constructed example connects the methodological discussion without presenting illustrative analysis as empirical findings. The chapter argues for an account of Arabic financial NLP in which linguistic context, documentary provenance and interpretive judgement remain part of the evidence throughout the analytical process.
evidence_items.title: Arabic Financial NLP

evidence_items.summary: Figurative language remains a major challenge for Machine Translation (MT) systems, as the intended meaning of such expressions often goes beyond literal translation. Although recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) improved the translation of Arabic dialects, benchmark resources for evaluating figurative language translation in Moroccan Darija remain scarce. To this end, we introduce the Moroccan Darija Figurative Language Corpus (MDFC), a benchmark dataset for MT and multiple-choice question (MCQ) selection covering idioms, metaphors, and proverbs. Using MDFC, we evaluate 19 open- and closed-weight language models and MT systems at both the expression and contextual levels under zero-shot and six-shot settings. We also conduct layer-wise similarity-based probing to determine how model representations distinguish figurative from literal meanings. Our findings reveal that closed-weight models achieve the strongest translation performance, while the benefits of contextual information vary across models and tasks. Differences between translation performance and MCQ accuracy highlight the distinction between generating an appropriate figurative translation and recognizing the intended meaning among candidate translations.
evidence_items.title: Towards Figurative Language Understanding in Moroccan Darija: An Evaluation of Large Language Models

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, preference data
evidence_items.summary: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. Our contribution includes two resources in English and Modern Standard Arabic: a culturally grounded preference dataset for training and evaluation, and a multiple-choice benchmark designed to assess culturally aligned behavior across nations. All test data are validated by native speakers to ensure authenticity. To optimize cultural alignment, we experiment with post-training methods across multilingual and Arabic-centric language models, evaluating performance on both generation tasks and our cultural multiple-choice benchmark. By releasing an evaluation benchmark, we provide a foundation for systematically studying and improving culturally aligned behavior in language models.
evidence_items.title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences

evidence_items.summary: Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $\rho \approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($\rho \approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.
evidence_items.title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation

rationale: Matched: agentic~bench, benchmark, evaluat, evaluation suite
evidence_items.summary: As LLM-based agents are deployed with increasing autonomy in real-world environments, a critical failure mode emerges: agentic misalignment, where agents choose harmful actions over failure. However, existing safety benchmarks primarily evaluate whether agents comply with explicitly harmful instructions, leaving the conditions that cause agents to choose harmful actions poorly understood. To address this limitation, we propose AM-Bench, a unified taxonomy and 35 scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries for agentic misalignment grounded in the fraud triangle, a well-established criminological framework explaining goal-directed misconduct. We adapt this framework to agentic environments and construct our evaluation suite and detection systems along three dimensions: perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning. We operationalize each dimension into structured subcategories rooted in prior theory: five threat categories derived from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories drawn from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four-question binary reasoning framework synthesized from prior literature. Our evaluation of 10 frontier models reveals a 62-percentage-point gap in misalignment across scenarios, with Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibiting the highest levels of agentic misalignment while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near-zero rates across all conditions. Our reasoning framework further reveals that models may exhibit harmful behaviours without explicit situational awareness or explanation, complicating both mitigation and detection. AM-Bench scenarios and code are available at https://github.com/AI4Collaboration/Agentic-Misalignment-Bench
evidence_items.title: AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment

evidence_items.summary: ASSETUKR is a Ukrainian translation of ASSET (Alva-Manchego et al., 2020), a benchmark for sentence simplification with multiple rewriting transformations. It is intended for validating and fine-tuning Ukrainian text simplification models. The dataset keeps the structure of ASSET: 2,000 validation and 359 test original sentences, each with 10 simplified variants. The text was translated with Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-uk, and the entire dataset was manually checked by two native Ukrainian speakers. Alignment with the English ASSET is preserved. Limitations: the data is translated from English, so its domain and style reflect the source, and the simplifications were written by English annotators. Previously available on GitHub: https://github.com/olgakanishcheva/Ukrainian-Text-Simplification/tree/main/ASSETUKR Citation: Kanishcheva, O. (2023). ASSETUKR: a Dataset for Ukrainian Text Simplification. LTC 2023.
evidence_items.title: ASSETUKR: A Ukrainian Dataset for Text Simplification and Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: This research dataset accompanies the manuscript Performance Impact of SQL Predicate Rewrites in Oracle Database by Andrea Meleková, Ivan Pastierik, and Michal Kvet. The dataset provides experimental benchmark results and reproducible SQL scripts for evaluating the performance impact of alternative SQL predicate formulations in Oracle Database 19c. The experiments examine execution time, CPU time, logical and physical reads, execution plans, access paths, and semantic equivalence across three dataset sizes containing approximately 1 million, 10 million, and 100 million rows. Repository contents: RW LAB SETUP FINAL 2026.sql – SQL/SQL Plus script for generating synthetic data, creating database objects and indexes, executing benchmark queries, and collecting performance metrics and execution plans. export novy 2026.xlsx – experimental benchmark results organized into worksheets for 1 million, 10 million, and 100 million rows. README.md – dataset documentation, experimental configuration, and reproduction instructions. LICENSE.txt – licensing information. Experimental environment: The experiments were conducted using Oracle Database 19c in an on-premises environment running Windows 11, with 32 GB RAM, a 4.70 GHz processor (16 logical CPUs), and NVMe storage. Each registered benchmark query was executed with 5 warm-up iterations and 30 measured repetitions. The experiments cover logical and membership predicates, subqueries, range and date conditions, scalar functions, NULL-sensitive expressions, data-type conversions, and semantic-equivalence checks. The accompanying SQL script supports reproduction of the experimental framework and can be configured for different dataset sizes. Execution times and execution plans may vary depending on hardware, database configuration, statistics, caching, and optimizer behavior.
evidence_items.title: Performance Impact of SQL Predicate Rewrites in Oracle Database: Benchmark Dataset and Reproduction Scripts

Results are split by reasoning mode: comparing a thinking-on (reasoning) model's quality against a thinking-off model is apples-to-oranges, so the two groups… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/witcheer/rtx-5090-benchmarks.

evidence_items.summary: CIOM-CI is an execution-level benchmark for learning-based test case prioritisation in continuous integration. It contains 523,885 test-class executions from 2,980 Travis CI jobs (2,003 commits) across 123 open-source Java projects, with 6,618 real failures, derived from the corpus of Peng et al. (ISSTA 2020) as repackaged by Li et al. (STVR 2024). Each execution carries an identifier-token description derived from the test's source code, a semantic score from a published classifier of implicit test cases, a BM25 relevance score between the build's code changes and the test, and execution-history features. The archive contains the dataset (ciom dataset.csv, zipped), a companion file of build-strict pre-execution features that remove information from concurrently running sibling jobs, the construction and evaluation code, the serialised classifier and its training corpus (TCdata), the anonymised materials of a three-rater labelling study, and the per-cycle results reported in the accompanying paper. The source corpus is not redistributed. See README.md for contents, checksums and reproduction steps, and DATASHEET.md for intended uses and known issues.
evidence_items.title: CIOM-CI: A leakage-audited benchmark of real continuous integration test executions with test text — dataset, code and labelling materials

evidence_items.summary: A Scholarly Knowledge Graph Benchmark Dataset | research | earth and nature | education | computer science | recommender systems | social networks
