evidence_items.summary: Audio description (AD) aims to enhance the accessibility of visual media for blind and low-vision (BLV) persons. However, in higher education, where slide-based lectures are a default mode of teaching, lecture AD remains largely underexplored. The main reason is that existing production guidelines, evaluation metrics, and benchmark datasets are oriented toward entertainment content and do not transfer to lectures, where ADs must complement the lecturer's speech, resolve deictic references, and fit within narrow pauses. In this work, we propose AD4Edu, consisting of an AD benchmark, AD4Edu-Bench, and a rule-diagnosable evaluation metric, AD4Edu-Eval, for generating and evaluating ADs in higher education. Specifically, we consolidated established accessibility guidance, including WCAG 2.2, the DCMP Description Key, and NCAM's STEM description practices. We further collected silver reference ADs, judge-ordered preference pairs, and pairwise preferences from four BLV raters, and post-trained models with direct preference optimization (DPO) for detailed analysis. Our findings indicate that while the metric reliably detects violations of the standard, ADs that comply with it do not necessarily fulfill the subjective preferences of BLV persons, most notably on description length, underscoring the necessity of active participation of BLV persons in co-designing inclusive AI solutions.
evidence_items.title: AD4EDU: Benchmarking University Lecture Audio Description across Accessibility Standards, Metrics, and Learner Preferences

evidence_items.summary: We study environment scaling as a way to increase agent-benchmark difficulty while holding core task objectives fixed. Our framework, Recursive Environment Scaling (RES), transforms existing benchmark environments while preserving their objectives and completion requirements. A proposer changes information access, resource relations, and execution dependencies; execution-grounded checks validate the resulting candidate, and accepted changes are inherited across rounds. This produces related environments for paired evaluation and training-trajectory collection. Experiments on 294 initial tasks from three benchmarks show lower task success for all six evaluation models, with decreases of 57.14--77.14 percentage points on Claw-Eval-Live. With equal trajectory counts and identical optimization settings, fine-tuning on RES trajectories outperforms original-trajectory SFT in all nine model--benchmark comparisons by 7.00--14.61 percentage points. Ablations identify recursive inheritance and dependency composition as important contributors to increased difficulty. Together, these results support environment scaling for both agent evaluation and training.
evidence_items.title: Recursive Environment Scaling for General Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: Agentic graph learning (AGL) has recently achieved promising results on graph reasoning tasks, where an agent powered by a large language model (LLM) sequentially samples the graph as evidence to support its final prediction. Existing methods either employ a single agent or orchestrate multiple role-based agents to reason and learn over the entire graph, but both essentially rely on a shared reasoning policy across different graph regions, which can be suboptimal for graphs with heterogeneous structural and semantic patterns. Inspired by the progress of multi-agent collaboration on complex reasoning tasks, a natural remedy is to let multiple agents own different memory and collaborate; however, applying this paradigm to graphs directly faces two challenges. First, existing AGL methods typically verbalize graph structures into natural-language descriptions for LLM agents, making the reasoning process sensitive to the ordering of structural information and thereby breaking the permutation-invariant nature of graphs. Second, incorporating increasingly large sampled neighborhoods leads to rapidly growing contexts. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a multi-agent agentic graph learning (i.e., MAAGL) framework. MAAGL partitions the graph into communities and assigns an independent agent to each community for region-specific specialization. MAAGL represents structural and semantic evidence separately. Structural evidence is summarized by a dynamically updated structural signature that is permutation-invariant and fixed in size, while semantic evidence is filtered to the top-k nodes ranked by relevance. Based on historical trajectories with similar signatures, agents estimate their confidence and trigger debate-style collaboration when needed. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets show that MAAGL outperforms SOTA AGL methods.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Agent Agentic Graph Learning via Structural Signatures

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is often evaluated with clean evidence, yet real retrieval can return topically relevant but unreliable content: false text and misleading images from corrupted metadata, entity swaps, typographic overlays, semantic edits, adversarial patches, blends, or style transfer. We introduce QIMG-7, a controlled benchmark for multimodal retrieval pollution in multi-sentence factual QA, spanning four datasets, seven image-attack families, and 16 paired clean/polluted regimes, for 1,760 evaluation rows per method. Across four generator/gate stacks, naive multimodal fusion is brittle: in the main gpt-4o-mini stack, Full-MM support drops from 0.908 with clean text to 0.490 with polluted text, often making Parametric fallback safer than retrieval. We propose source-aware trust resolution (SATR), a training-free approach that compares Parametric, Text-only, and Full-MM candidate answers and selects among candidate answers or falls back based on source reliability. The Field-Selector variant achieves the best balanced score, 0.816, improving over Full-MM by 11.7 points and over the Cascaded Router by 2.7 points. Ablations show that, in this text-first setting, explicit text-reliability modeling is the dominant driver of these gains. Overall, in text-first factual QA with multimodal retrieval conflict, our results support selective trust rather than unconditional fusion. Artifacts are available at https://github.com/SaadElDine/Trust_Before_Fusion.
evidence_items.title: Trust Before Fusion: QIMG-7 and Source-Aware Resolution for Polluted Multimodal RAG

evidence_items.summary: Current evaluation protocols for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in Radiology Report Generation (RRG) rely on report-level metrics that measure lexical overlap or aggregate clinical correctness. However, such metrics do not test whether individual diagnostic statements stem from the actual pathological evidence visible in the image. This allows models to achieve competitive scores by exploiting learned priors or spurious correlations, a failure mode we refer to as vision shortcut. We introduce SHOVIR, a benchmark for evaluating vision shortcut behavior in RRG. SHOVIR extends two spatially annotated chest X-ray datasets, MIMIC-CXR and PadChest-GR, with per-box CheXpert labels, and defines image-level and disease-level occlusion experiments that contrast baseline performance on clean images against localized, region-specific perturbations. Comparing predictions across these conditions isolates two failure modes at the disease-class level: direct shortcuts, where a finding persists after its visual evidence is removed, and contextual shortcuts, where detection degrades once co-occurring pathologies are occluded despite the target region remaining intact. Benchmarking eight state-of-the-art VLMs, we find that shortcut behavior varies substantially across architectures and datasets. Models achieving the highest baseline report quality do not necessarily rank highest in spatial grounding, revealing that clinically fluent generation can coexist with shallow reliance on visual evidence. These findings expose a blind spot in current RRG evaluation and motivate region-aware assessment protocols.
evidence_items.title: SHOVIR: A Benchmark for Evaluating Vision Shortcut Learning in Radiology Report Generation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that reason over documents rather than answer from parametric knowledge. We study archive-grounded reasoning: locating sparse evidence across a large, messy collection of workplace files, reconciling inconsistent terminology, units, and time conventions, and computing an answer. Existing benchmarks address only parts of this setting and none jointly stresses archive-groundedness, agentic exploration, and cross-domain coverage. We introduce Agora, a benchmark pairing 362 questions with eight domain collections of 9,664 authentic documents and 372M tokens, far exceeding any model's context window, so agents must explore deliberately rather than scan exhaustively. Agora is built by an agentic pipeline combining cross-document task synthesis, leakage-preventing obfuscation, and difficulty filtering. Evaluating eight models, we find the task far from solved: even the strongest reaches only 59.4% accuracy, with notable variation across domains.
evidence_items.title: AGORA: An Archive-Grounded Benchmark for Agentic Workplace Document Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Proof autoformalization aims to translate a mathematical informal proof in natural language into a formal proof in a formal language such as Lean 4. Existing LLM-based models for proof autoformalization are typically evaluated only on well-formed informal proofs from curated datasets. We argue that a robust proof autoformalizer must remain faithful even for informal proofs that diverge from these idealized ones, and we present the first study on the robustness of proof autoformalization models. We formulate two categories of perturbations: a global perturbation paraphrases the informal theorem-proof pair in a different style, under which the formalization should remain consistent; a local perturbation alters a value, symbol, or proof step, possibly in a counterfactual way, and a robust formalization should faithfully reflect the perturbation rather than reverting to the original or inferring a different one on its own. We build a benchmark with both perturbations on miniF2F and MATH-500, and automatically measure how stable a proof autoformalization's correctness is under global perturbations and how faithfully its output reflects local perturbations. We evaluate seven recent models: their correctness varies under global perturbations, and they mostly fail to remain faithful under local perturbations.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4

evidence_items.summary: Although it is generally agreed that AI-generated text poses a broad societal risk, there is no common understanding in the AI-generated text detection literature on what constitutes harmful use. Rather, existing datasets and approaches often define their own criteria and make their own assumptions, sometimes implicitly, and often only loosely related to real-world needs and applications. To address this gap, we here systematically define various notions of AI-generated text and their characteristics. To study these, we collect AITDNA - a new benchmark of human-machine co-constructed texts that is annotated with detailed genesis information, such as the entire edit and AI-interaction history. We benchmark various machine-generated text detectors and find that they often only perform well for specific notions but not as broad detectors. We release code and data publicly.
evidence_items.title: 'Your AI Text is not Mine': Redefining and Evaluating AI-generated Text Detection under Realistic Assumptions

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) seek to improve reasoning by combining diverse perspectives from multiple agents. However, aggregation may overlook supportive, contradictory, and uncertain relations among their responses. As a result, useful dissent can be suppressed, allowing an incorrect majority to dominate the final decision. We introduce SIGMA, a novel Signed Graph-informed Multi-Agent reasoning framework that distinguishes support, contradiction, and uncertainty among responses from black-box LLM agents. SIGMA constructs a signed evidence graph, reassesses disputed relations, and forms reasoning communities while preserving distinct evidence. It then conducts bounded cross-examination between community representatives and adjudicates their evidence without treating community size as a proxy for correctness. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets, across multiple LLM backbones and diverse multi-agent configurations, demonstrate that SIGMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving notable gains in both accuracy and conflict-resilient performance.
evidence_items.title: Conflict-Aware Multi-Agent Reasoning via Signed Graph Modeling

evidence_items.summary: Operational disaster response goes beyond damage assessment, requiring responders to integrate multi-sensor signals, reason over road networks, populations and key facilities, plan evacuations, and produce actionable reports. However, prior work largely isolates remote-sensing perception or evaluates generic tool use, leaving the end-to-end workflows of emergency operations underexplored. In this paper, we introduce Disaster Operational Response Agent benchmark (DORA), the first agentic benchmark for end-to-end disaster response: 515 expert-authored tasks across 45 real-world disaster events spanning 10 types, paired with expert-verified, replayable gold trajectories totaling 3,500 tool-call steps. Tasks span five dimensions that cover the operational disaster-response pipeline: disaster perception, spatial relational analysis, rescue and evacuation planning, temporal evolution reasoning, and multi-modal report synthesis. Agents compose calls from a 108-tool MCP library over heterogeneous geospatial data: optical, SAR, and multi-spectral imagery across single-, bi-, and multi-temporal sequences (0.015-10m GSD), complemented by elevation and social vector layers. We comprehensively evaluate 13 frontier LLMs on our benchmark, revealing three persistent challenges: 1) disaster-domain grounding exposes unique failure modes (damage-semantic grounding, sensor-modality mismatch, and disaster-pipeline composition); 2) agents are doubly bottlenecked by tool selection and argument grounding, where gold tool-order hints improve accuracy by only 1.08-4.40%, and alternative scaffolds yield at most a 3.24% gain; 3) compositional fragility scales with trajectory length, the agent-to-gold gap widening from 7% to 56% on long pipelines. DORA establishes a rigorous testbed for operationally reliable disaster-response agents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Junjue-Wang/DORA.
evidence_items.title: Can LLM Agents Respond to Disasters? Benchmarking Heterogeneous Geospatial Reasoning in Emergency Operations

evidence_items.summary: High-throughput, effective and comprehensive phenotyping is a critical prerequisite for crop improvement. While phenotypic analysis was traditionally performed manually, recent advances in multimodal foundation models, especially in vision-language models, have offered new opportunities for automated plant phenotyping. However, plant science remains particularly challenging for general-purpose VLMs because it requires domain-specific knowledge, fine-grained visual interpretation, and complex agronomic reasoning. We introduce PlantXpert, an evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning benchmark for plant phenotyping across four major crops: soybean, cotton, rice, and corn. Our benchmark provides a structured and reproducible framework for agronomic adaptation of VLMs, and enables controlled comparison between base models and their domain-adapted counterparts. We constructed a dataset comprising 545 digital images and 4,351 benchmark samples spanning key agronomic domains including disease, pest control, weed management and yield. The benchmark can assess diverse capabilities including visual expertise, quantitative reasoning, and multi-step agronomic reasoning. We trained and evaluated a total of 11 state-of-the-art VLMs. Fine-tuning on our dataset improves overall accuracy for all models, with many achieving around 70% accuracy, and improvements on 9 of 11 remaining statistically significant after Holm correction. We also identify diminishing returns from model scaling, uneven performance across crop subsets, and persistent weaknesses in quantitative reasoning and specialized image analysis. These limitations show that general multimodal competence alone is insufficient for reliable agronomic reasoning and demonstrate the value of domain-specific adaptation. We hope PlantXpert can serve as a foundation for advancing evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in plant science.
evidence_items.title: From Scientific Crop Imagery to Agronomic Reasoning: A Multimodal LLM Benchmark for Plant Phenotyping

evidence_items.summary: Accurate estimation of forest biomass, a major carbon sink, relies heavily on tree-level traits such as height and species. Unoccupied Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) capturing high-resolution imagery from a single RGB camera offer a cost-effective and scalable approach for mapping and measuring individual trees. We introduce BIRCH-Trees, the first benchmark for individual tree height and species estimation from tree-centered UAV images, spanning three datasets: temperate forests, tropical forests, and boreal plantations. We also present DINOvTree, a unified approach using a Vision Foundation Model (VFM) backbone with task-specific heads for simultaneous height and species prediction. Through extensive evaluations on BIRCH-Trees, we compare DINOvTree against commonly used vision methods, including VFMs, as well as biological allometric equations. We find that DINOvTree achieves top overall results with accurate height predictions and competitive classification accuracy while using only 54% to 58% of the parameters of the second-best approach.
evidence_items.title: Estimating Individual Tree Height and Species from UAV Imagery

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent peer reviews but often miss sparse, subtle, and document-level scientific errors. We introduce PaperAudit-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating paper-level error detection and error-aware automated review. It comprises (1) PaperAudit-Dataset, 220 high-quality AI/ML papers containing more than 2,200 controlled synthetic errors across eight categories, and (2) PaperAudit-Review, an evidence-aware framework that links structured error detection to review generation. Experiments across models, error categories, paper sections, and analysis depths show that sparse long-context auditing remains challenging for current LLMs. Conditioning review generation on explicit, manuscript-grounded error evidence produces more conservative and discriminative assessments that align more closely with human judgments than representative automated-review baselines. The dataset also supports post-training compact detectors through SFT and RL; Qwen3-14B achieves 55.8% F1 at Detection@1 under a fixed held-out protocol. A PubPeer transfer study and deployment in ScienceOne, a scientific foundation-model platform led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, further illustrate practical applicability. Code and Dataset Page: https://github.com/TU2021/PaperAudit ScienceOne Manuscript Review: https://www.scienceone.cn/lit/#/assistant
evidence_items.title: PaperAudit-Bench: Benchmarking Error Detection in Research Papers for Critical Automated Peer Review

evidence_items.summary: Leveraging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to develop embodied agents offers significant promise for addressing complex real-world tasks. However, current evaluation benchmarks remain predominantly language-centric or heavily reliant on simulated environments, rarely probing the nuanced, knowledge-intensive reasoning essential for practical, real-world scenarios. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce the task of Sparsely Grounded Visual Navigation, explicitly designed to evaluate the sequential decision-making abilities of MLLMs in challenging, knowledge-intensive real-world environment. We operationalize this task with CityNav, a comprehensive benchmark encompassing four diverse global cities, specifically constructed to assess raw MLLM-driven agents in city navigation. Agents are required to rely solely on visual inputs and internal multimodal reasoning to sequentially navigate 50+ decision points without additional environmental annotations or specialized architectural modifications. Crucially, agents must autonomously achieve localization through interpreting city-specific cues and recognizing landmarks, perform spatial reasoning, and strategically plan and execute routes to their destinations. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that current state-of-the-art MLLMs, reasoning techniques (e.g., GEPA, chain-of-thought, reflection) and competitive baseline PReP significantly underperform in this challenging setting. To address this, we propose Verbalization of Path(VoP), which explicitly grounds the agent's internal reasoning by probing city-scale cognitive maps (key landmarks and directions toward the destination) from the MLLM, substantially enhancing navigation success. Project Webpage: https://dwipddalal.github.io/AgentNav/
evidence_items.title: Can MLLMs Find Their Way in a City? Exploring Emergent Navigation from Web-Scale Knowledge

evidence_items.summary: Harness-side learning methods such as reflection and prompt evolution let an LLM agent improve from outcome feedback without updating its weights. In finance the natural feedback is a market or policy outcome, and such an outcome is a useful reward only when the documents the agent reads carry learnable information about it. We report a verified benchmark for outcome-guided reading of Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) minutes, built on Cieslak and Vissing-Jorgensen's study of the "Fed put," the Federal Reserve's tendency to ease policy after poor stock-market performance. The benchmark contains 1,197 equity-market passages from the minutes of 200 meetings (2000-2024), fixed chronological splits, an audited reconstruction of the authors' automated phrase-and-direction method, and the authors' human-coded tone counts, which we recover from their published figures. Screening two candidate rewards with frozen readers (fixed models and instructions) gives opposite answers. The equity return that preceded a meeting is learnable from the minutes. A frozen embedding recovers it with an out-of-sample R^2 of 0.50, and tone labels from a frozen LLM reach 0.49, against 0.32 for a linear readout of the reconstructed phrase-and-direction counts. The next change in the policy rate shows no detectable signal. In a test specified before estimation, no text representation beats a baseline without text. A pilot with a frozen LLM reader exposes a credit-assignment problem. One crisis meeting accounts for 79% of the pilot's feedback error, although the reader labels all of its passages negative, the correct direction. An LLM reflector that rewrites the reader's instructions from outcome residuals would therefore be pushed to change labels whose direction is already right. We release the environment, comparators, and a validation-gated adaptation protocol. We have not yet run the adaptive comparisons. Also available on SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=7626078.
evidence_items.title: Which Outcome Should Teach an LLM Reader? A Verified FOMC Benchmark and Reward-Design Evidence for Outcome-Guided Agents in Finance

evidence_items.summary: Outlier detection is often run on a random sample because the full dataset is too large. This repository measures resilience to sampling: whether a detector flags the same records when it is fitted on a simple random sample (without replacement) as when it is fitted on the full dataset. Two label-free measures are used: Dice resilience ρ, the overlap of the two flagged lists of equal size, and rank resilience ρ̃, the Spearman correlation of the two score vectors. The accompanying paper groups 18 detectors into four classes by the statistic their scores depend on, and derives how resilience depends on the sample size and the sampling fraction for each class. The experiments (E1–E8, with E1b and E2b) use 16 benchmark datasets of up to 286,048 records, 13 further datasets for the convergence experiments, and synthetic data. Main result: at a 10% sampling fraction, detectors built on the k-nearest-neighbour graph (Class IV: LOF, KNN, ABOD, Feature Bagging, ADOD) kept on average 48% of their flagged records. The other three classes kept 76% to 82%. Class IV was the least resilient class on all 16 datasets (Friedman test with datasets as blocks, χ²(3) = 32.5, p = 4.2×10⁻⁷). The repository contains the code, the configuration, the result of every replicate, and the scripts that produce every table and figure of the paper. Version 3.0.0 accompanies the revised manuscript. The folder archive/submitted version holds the earlier analysis, which is superseded.
evidence_items.title: Outlier Detection Methods Are Not Equally Resilient to Sampling

evidence_items.summary: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories. We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation. To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a state-transition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, model-ensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts. Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answer-only evaluation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/FinHopper/.
evidence_items.title: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the paper "The Impostors Method as a Statistical Test for Authorship Verification With Large Language Models as Sampling Source for Hard Negatives", presented at EMNLP 2026. It contains the Blog Posts data used in our experiments, the corresponding LLM-generated paraphrases, and the authorship verification pairings used for evaluating the Impostors Method. The release is intended to facilitate reproduction of the experiments and further research on authorship verification, impostor generation, and LLM-based paraphrasing. The original texts originate from the Blog Authorship Corpus introduced by Schler et al. (2006), which consists of English blog posts collected from Blogger.com before September 2004. In our experiments, the corpus was preprocessed and text pairs were constructed while controlling for topic, year, gender, and author age. The archive contains: Original Blog Posts texts used in the experiments. LLM-generated paraphrases produced using the paraphrasing approaches investigated in the paper, including one-step and two-step generation. Pair definitions / pair IDs specifying the same-author and different-author document pairs used in the authorship verification experiments. The LLM-generated paraphrases were created as potential impostor documents, i.e., hard negatives for the Impostors Method. The generation approaches aim to preserve relevant contextual properties of the source documents while varying their linguistic realization. Original dataset reference J. Schler, M. Koppel, S. Argamon and J. Pennebaker (2006). Effects of Age and Gender on Blogging in Proceedings of 2006 AAAI Spring Symposium on Computational Approaches for Analyzing Weblogs. Paper Klara M. Gutekunst, Yaron Winter, and Martin Potthast. 2026. The Impostors Method as a Statistical Test for Authorship Verification With Large Language Models as Sampling Source for Hard Negatives. EMNLP 2026.

authors: Kaiwei Chen, Moran Li, Zhenye Gan, Yabiao Wang, Chengjie Wang, Kexin Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
evidence_items.summary: Recent video generation models produce visually compelling outputs, yet their physical plausibility remains poorly measured. Physical plausibility asks whether generated objects obey geometry, kinematics, dynamics, and conservation laws. Existing benchmarks rely on coarse visual-language model judgments or target embodied world models rather than video generation itself. We introduce PVBench, a physical video benchmark that quantitatively measures the plausibility of generated videos across 46 dimensions organized into seven domains, spanning: i) instruction and semantic fidelity, ii) behavioral and causal consistency, iii) perceptual and temporal quality, iv) geometric and spatial consistency, v) material properties and field states, vi) kinematic and spatiotemporal persistence, vii) and mechanical plausibility with conservation laws. PVBench comprises 600 carefully crafted prompts, of which 30% involve physical embodied agents such as robot arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and multi-agent systems. For challenging physically tractable dimensions, it pairs each with specialized vision models that derive verifiable, physically grounded measurements, such as object-level 6D pose, metric scale, surface normals, kinematics, and numerical conservation-law residuals. It thus avoids relying solely on subjective scoring, while supporting both text-to-video and image-to-video generation. Finally, we validate the agreement between automatic metrics and human judgments through human evaluation. Meanwhile, we evaluate mainstream open-source and closed-source models and present several insights. By releasing the benchmark, prompts, and calibration protocol, we aim to foster physically grounded video generation.
evidence_items.title: PVBench: Quantifying Physical Plausibility in Video Generation with Object-Level Physical Measurements

evidence_items.summary: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.
evidence_items.title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise

evidence_items.summary: Proactive agents can support group collaboration by surfacing useful information without waiting to be asked, but even relevant contributions can be disruptive if poorly timed. In this work, we isolate the timing question: given a fixed candidate contribution such as a clarification or relevant fact, when should an AI agent chime in? We introduce PITCH (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat), to our knowledge the first benchmark with large-scale human judgments of proactive agent timing collected from participants in the same unscripted multi-party conversations they took part in. To collect high-quality judgments, we design a novel interface in which 2-4 people chat synchronously, author candidate AI contribution messages, place their own and others' contributions into the chat history, and then deliberate as a group about the best placement for each message. PITCH contains 384 candidate contributions and 1,091 judgments, each marking an ideal turn, an acceptable window, or that a contribution should not appear, from 89 participants engaged in 35 conversations. Evaluating 15 models across 28 configurations, we find that while models can place contributions well when given the entire conversation history, they systematically chime in too early when asked to decide live as the conversation unfolds: best-turn accuracy falls from 57.8% to 19.0%, with nearly half of placements occurring before every participant's acceptable window. In comparison, lay humans deciding live are more accurate (23.7% vs 19.0%), and fewer of their placements are premature (39.7% vs 46.4%). Model reasoning traces show that 93% of intervention justifications cite relevance, while almost none consider waiting. By providing a human-grounded benchmark, our work reveals gaps in agents' ability to integrate into group settings and points towards proactive agents that can reason explicitly about appropriate timing.
evidence_items.title: When Should AI Chime In? Benchmarking Timely Contribution of Proactive Agents in Multi-Party Chat

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real-world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well-calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). This raises a key question: are these objectives sufficient to guide agents toward models that meet the broader requirements of real-world medical use? In this study, we introduce Auto-MD-bench, a benchmark of 15 real-world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, spanning survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. We evaluate four agents: AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch. The strongest agents achieve competitive primary scores, yet their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of the simple baseline models, which could lead to severe medical accidents. Moreover, models with nearly identical primary scores can exhibit markedly different calibration, while performance varies substantially across population shifts. These findings show that primary task performance alone is insufficient to assess autonomous clinical modeling and multiple different metrics widely used in healthcare practice need to be taken into consideration.
evidence_items.title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks

organizations: Alfred-Wegener-Institut Helmholtz-Zentrum für Polar- und Meeresforschung
evidence_items.summary: The measurement of ice thickness is of great importance for the accurate estimation of glacier volume and the delineation of their bedrock topography. In particular, this is a crucial factor in forecasting the future evolution of glaciers in the context of a changing climate. In order to derive the ice thickness, the travel time of electromagnetic waves in radargrams acquired by radio-echo sounding (RES) systems is analyzed. This can only be achieved by identifying the ice surface and underlying ice bottom in corresponding radargrams. Manually identifying these two reflection horizons in RES data is a laborious and time-consuming process. Consequently, scientists are attempting to automate this task through the use of techniques such as deep learning. Such automation can significantly reduce the time between a field campaign and the calculation of the glacier's ice thickness distribution. In this paper, we present the first benchmark dataset for delineating the ice surface and bottom boundaries in RES data, to facilitate straightforward comparisons of deep learning models in the future. The IceAnatomy'' dataset comprises radargrams and the corresponding manual picks, amounting to a total of over 45,000km of observations. The RES data originates from three sources: FAU, CReSIS, and AWI. The dataset comprises different RES systems as well as different pre-processing methods. In addition, the data was acquired over a large range of geographical and glaciological settings, featuring different thermal regimes present in Antarctica and the Southern Patagonian Icefield. This diversity ensures that the models' behaviors can be analyzed in different scenarios. We define a standardized train-test split for each source in the dataset. This allows us to introduce not only a baseline model trained on the entire training set (the omni'' model), but also three source-specific baseline models.
evidence_items.title: Ice Anatomy: A Benchmark Dataset and Methodology for Automatic Ice Boundary Extraction from Radio-Echo Sounding Data

evidence_items.summary: Java applications reach large language models (LLMs) through an integration framework, and rely on it to handle a failing provider: to retry what can be retried and nothing else, to wait as long as the provider asks, never to present a truncated answer as complete, and to record each failure in the application's metrics. We state these expectations as a six-clause reliability contract and measure Spring AI 2.0.1 and LangChain4j 1.21.0 against it with a scripted OpenAI-compatible provider: fifteen failure scenarios, synchronous and streaming, three repetitions. LangChain4j meets it in 47 of 77 applicable cases with its defaults and in 51 of 83 when configured explicitly, Spring AI in 72 of 77 and 76 of 83; both deliver a stream that ended without its terminator as a complete answer. We then place one implementation of the contract beneath both frameworks, at the HTTP boundary - an OkHttp interceptor for Spring AI, an HttpClient for LangChain4j, and a java.net.http transport for code without a framework - sharing a 725-line core that depends only on the JDK and the Micrometer Observation API. With it, all three clients behave identically and meet the contract in 90 of 91 cases; the remaining case is a policy trade-off between retrying a hung provider and waiting for a slow first token. Against a local model server the layer rejected none of 700 calls, and it adds a median of 32-217 microseconds to a call.
evidence_items.title: Consistent LLM Call Handling Across Java Frameworks: A Reference Implementation and Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Language model benchmarks assign each question a single outcome from one fixed wording, even though the same underlying request can be expressed in many equivalent ways. We argue that the quantity of interest should therefore not be correctness on one wording, but the accessibility of an inquiry, which we define as the probability that a model succeeds across meaning-preserving formulations. The distribution of accessibility across inquiries reveals a structure that accuracy and existing best-, worst-, or average-case prompt scores collapse: how broadly a model's capabilities extend across inquiries and how dependably those capabilities can be elicited. Two models can have the same average performance while one succeeds across more inquiries unreliably and the other succeeds across fewer inquiries but more consistently, leading to opposite preferences depending on whether the task allows multiple retries until one success or when repeated consistent success is required. Across six benchmarks and more than twenty models, this tradeoff is common: for about half of the model pairs with nearly equal mean accessibility, which model looks better depends on whether one success across five formulations is enough or all five must succeed, quantities we call Access@5 and Reliable@5, respectively. For some pairs the two measures diverge significantly, by up to 10 points in opposite directions. Accessibility also reveals that scaling, reasoning, and prompt optimization can redistribute capability across inquiries in ways aggregate accuracy obscures, sometimes broadening the set of inquiries a model can succeed on while making success on them less repeatable. Accessibility turns formulation sensitivity from a nuisance into a measurable property of capability, distinguishing what a model can sometimes succeed on from what users can actually depend on.
evidence_items.title: Revealing what benchmark scores hide: Jointly measuring the breadth and reliability of LLM capabilities using accessibility profiles

evidence_items.summary: Dozens of deep architectures for time-series anomaly detection have been published since 2018, most of them reporting higher scores than their predecessors on the same handful of datasets. A series of critical studies now suggests that much of this progress is an artefact. The datasets have flaws that make them easy or mislabelled. The most common scoring protocol, point adjustment, inflates results so strongly that random scores can compete with trained models. And when classical or deliberately simple methods are run under the same conditions, they often match the deep ones. This review assembles that evidence. We describe the method families briefly, then examine the benchmark critiques, the evaluation metrics and their failure modes, and the large comparison studies. A small worked example, constructed by hand and labelled as such, shows the arithmetic of point adjustment. We end with a reporting checklist and with the open question of whether pretrained time-series models change the picture. Apart from that worked example, no new result is reported.
evidence_items.title: Time-Series Anomaly Detection: Benchmark Flaws, Evaluation Metrics and Strong Baselines

evidence_items.summary: The discovery of new solid-state ionic conductors remains challenging because ion transport depends sensitively on both mobile-ion chemistry and the host crystal framework. Although atomistic calculations can evaluate migration barriers directly, simple descriptors can greatly facilitate screening large materials spaces and gaining mechanistic insight. However, existing descriptors often show limited transferability across mobile-ion chemistries and material classes. Here, we generate a diverse dataset of ion-migration barriers spanning Li-, Na-, K-, and Mg-ion conductors across oxides, sulfides, and halides, and use it to systematically benchmark descriptors. From this analysis, we devise distance contraction, ∆d, a simple local geometric descriptor that measures the largest contraction of mobile-ion-neighbor distances relative to their equilibrium values along a migration pathway. This quantity captures the dominant short-range repulsion penalty associated with ion migration and consistently distinguishes low- from high-barrier pathways across chemistries. Using ∆d in a high-throughput screening workflow, we recover many known fast-ion conductors and identify previously unexplored candidates, with fast-ion transport validated by nudged elastic band calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics simulations. Beyond screening, ∆d links diverse ion-transport mechanisms to a common physical quantity: The largest distance contraction experienced by the migrating ion.
evidence_items.title: A Simple Descriptor for Solid-State Ionic Conductors Across Chemistries.

evidence_items.summary: Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback for policy learning and execution monitoring. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Our results reveal errors in fine-grained instruction grounding, history-dependent progress tracking, and recovery assessment, even in models with strong outcome and forward-progress scores. The same semantic subtask can also receive substantially different value gains across valid execution orders. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. The website is available at https://robovalue-benchmark.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models

evidence_items.summary: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observer's motion, surrounding geometry, and hand-object interactions must fit together in a consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EgoXperience, a full-stack paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EgoX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EgoX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EgoX, trained with EgoX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in a shared world coordinate frame with a single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%.
evidence_items.title: EgoXperience: Learning World-Grounded Egocentric Representations from Human Experience

evidence_items.summary: Background Identifying individuals on parole or probation can help inform care pathways and ensure continuity of care in health care systems. However, this sensitive justice-related information is often absent from structured electronic health record fields and is instead documented in narrative clinical notes. Developing automated parole and probation detection (PPD) systems typically requires expert-annotated clinical data, but manual annotation is costly, time-consuming, and constrained by data sparsity and privacy concerns. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate a synthetic-only training paradigm for PPD from clinical text that eliminates the need for expert-annotated training data while maintaining strong performance and cross-domain transfer to real-world data. Methods We developed Synth-PPD, a synthetic dataset comprising 7579 labeled clinical notes generated using large language models (LLMs), redundancy filtering, and automated quality evaluation. Dataset quality was assessed through human review of 1517 synthetic notes by 2 annotators. The primary outcome was the macro–F1-score for PPD. We evaluated Synth-PPD across unsupervised and supervised learning settings using LLMs, traditional machine learning models, and transformer encoders. Performance was assessed on 293 expert-annotated real-world clinical notes from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. Results Synth-PPD achieved 90.05% human-LLM alignment. In the unsupervised setting, Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct with chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot examples from Synth-PPD achieved a macro–F1-score of 87.22%, outperforming both the corresponding zero-shot model (80.10%) and the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; P<.001 for all comparisons).
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Generated Synthetic Data for Parole and Probation Detection in Clinical Notes: Development and Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: Log parsing turns free-text log lines into event templates and is the first step of most log-mining pipelines, yet parser behavior on mobile-platform logs remains poorly characterized. We present ABRLogParser, a multi-parser benchmark that expands the ABRLog Android bug-report dataset by applying thirteen classical parsers to its eight regular-expression block types: 342 files, 14 devices, 32.0 million log lines. Every (file, parser) pair yields a released structured output and template summary, and each parser is characterized by content (how aggressively it abstracts lines into templates) and by execution (coverage, failure modes, runtime). Abstraction spans a factor of 906 across parsers and throughput about fiftyfold; parsers carrying the LogPAI server-log defaults degenerate into near-identity transforms on Android; and we map where each one breaks down on large inputs. The corpus has no ground-truth templates, so the artifact is a substrate for parser comparison, not an accuracy benchmark.
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Parser Benchmark over Android Bug-Report Logs

evidence_items.summary: Perturbation prediction models - which forecast transcriptional responses to gene inactivation - are increasingly proposed as in silico surrogates for genome-scale drug discovery screens. Yet, rigorous evaluation of whether these models genuinely generalize beyond their training distribution has been lacking. Existing benchmarks rely predominantly on random train-test splits, obscuring systematic failure modes that only emerge under realistic out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. Here we introduce EL-PERTURB (Extrapolative Learning for PERTURBation Prediction), a benchmarking framework that stress-tests 20 perturbation prediction models spanning six architecture classes on both essential gene and genome-wide Perturb-seq screens, using a novel stratified OOD splitting strategy that partitions train and test sets into functionally distinct regions of transcriptional space. We find that model performance degrades substantially under OOD conditions, and that architectural complexity - including single-cell foundation model embeddings - confers no reliable advantage over well-tuned simpler baselines. EL-PERTURB establishes a rigorous benchmark for perturbation effect prediction across a gradient of generalization difficulty, providing a guide for building models that can genuinely serve as surrogates for wet-lab screening.
evidence_items.title: Genetic Perturbation Prediction Models Fail Out-of-Distribution: A Rigorous Benchmark and Systematic Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: This study proposes a supervised Natural Language Processing approach based on BERTimbau to classify public expenditure liquidation records according to the descriptive sufficiency of their content. The research is grounded on the premise that generic, vague, or overly document-dependent descriptions reduce transparency and hinder institutional and social oversight of public spending. A labeled dataset of 600 records was constructed by random sampling with artificial class balancing from a corpus of 4,083 permanent equipment liquidation records from the State Executive Branch of Mato Grosso, Brazil, for fiscal year 2025, with labeling validated by two independent auditors via Cohen’s Kappa (κ = 0.900). Three supervised strategies were evaluated under stratified 10-fold cross-validation: TF-IDF + SVM (baseline), BERTimbau Feature-Based, and BERTimbau Fine-Tuning. The results demonstrate that both BERTimbau configurations outperformed the baseline with medium-to-large effect sizes, significant for Feature-Based, with Fine-Tuning achieving macro-F1 of 92.66% and accuracy of 92.67%, confirming the feasibility of contextualized Portuguese-language models for supporting preventive, risk-focused governmental auditing.
evidence_items.title: Classification of Descriptive Sufficiency in Public Expenditure Liquidation Records

evidence_items.summary: Automatic evaluation of abstractive summarization remains challenging because traditional lexical-overlap metrics often fail to capture semantic adequacy and factual consistency. This work proposes a composite evaluation metric integrating lexical, semantic, and factual dimensions. Metrics from each family are combined using a hierarchical weighted formulation, with both intra-family and inter-family weights optimized via Bayesian Optimization using the SummEval benchmark [Fabbri et al., 2021]. The resulting metric assigns 19% weight to lexical overlap, 58% to semantic similarity, and 23% to factuality, and achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.488 on the test set, outperforming the best individual metric, BERTScore-Precision (0.467). These results indicate that combining complementary evaluation dimensions yields a more robust and human-aligned signal for abstractive summarization.
evidence_items.title: A Composite Metric for Abstractive Summarization Evaluation: Integrating Lexical, Semantic, and Factual Dimensions

evidence_items.summary: Overview This repository provides the source code and trained model checkpoints for DG-PF + DPTR , a lightweight semantic segmentation network developed for autonomous latex collection bowl manipulation. The proposed method integrates two components: Difference-Guided Perception Fusion (DG-PF): A feature fusion component designed to improve the integration of semantic and spatial information. Difference-Guided Pixel-Wise Transfer Refinement (DPTR): A refinement component designed to improve segmentation predictions through difference-guided feature processing. The network employs a lightweight ResNet18-based encoder and processes RGB images at a resolution of 512 × 512 pixels. Segmentation Categories The network predicts six semantic categories: Bowl body ( bowl body ) Bowl mouth ( bowl mouth ) Empty bowl ( bowl empty ) Liquid ( liquid ) Bucket ( bucket ) Bucket mouth ( bucket mouth ) Repository Contents The software package provides the proposed segmentation architecture, training and evaluation code, inference utilities, trained model checkpoints, and implementation instructions. Application The segmentation method was developed to support RGB-D visual perception for agricultural robotic manipulation, particularly the autonomous handling of latex collection bowls. The corresponding annotated image dataset and indoor/outdoor robotic experiment implementations are intended to be released as separate research resources. Reproducibility Researchers can use the provided code and pretrained checkpoints to reproduce the segmentation methodology and conduct further evaluations. Instructions for installation, model loading, and execution are provided in the accompanying README file.
evidence_items.title: DG-PF + DPTR: A Lightweight Semantic Segmentation Network for Autonomous Latex Collection Bowl Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: This Data Descriptor presents normal-incidence acoustic measurements of thirty-two specimen configurations combining perforated plates having stepwise apertures with sheet-type triply periodic minimal surface cores. Eight perforated face-sheets, differing in aperture diameter and in the axial length of each aperture section, were each measured with an empty backing cavity and with cores of Schwarz Primitive, Gyroid and Diamond topology. Measurements were made by the two-microphone transfer function method in a 100 mm impedance tube from 50 Hz to 1600 Hz at 2 Hz resolution, with three acquisitions per configuration. For every configuration the dataset provides the sound absorption coefficient and the complex reflection coefficient, normalised surface impedance and normalised surface admittance, as individual repeats and as their mean, together with the unmodified instrument exports. The three core geometries are deposited as STL models, and all tabulated core parameters were measured from those models rather than taken from design targets. Repeatability, internal consistency, the recommended frequency range and the known limitations of the specimens and the measurement are documented. Version 2.0: corrected processing and geometry scripts, per-acquisition consistency check; see README, ‘Changes in this version’.

In a monthly leader–follower model, a stylised, predominantly deposit-funded euro-area bank chooses deposit rates, lending margins and the composition of bond reinvestment, while depositors and borrowers respond to these decisions and to economic conditions. The initial balance sheet is calibrated to selected indicators from regulatory disclosures. We estimate equation-based approximations of LLM-generated decisions and evaluate them against simulations not used in estimation. Across ten out-of-sample bank-year simulations, the final specification reproduces annual return on equity (ROE) within 0.31 percentage points and meets all fit criteria in seven; none of the deposit-run scenarios meets all criteria. In eighteen simulations with a second LLM family, the ROE difference does not exceed 0.71 percentage points, but only six meet all criteria. Against a market-pricing rule, the original optimisation model, and regression and nearest-neighbour approximations estimated on the same data, the final specification meets all criteria in more years and tracks liquidity most closely in deposit-run years. Instructions without behavioural guidance show that withdrawal magnitudes and fixed-rate borrowers’ price sensitivity depend materially on the instructions supplied; with customer equations estimated under neutral instructions, a two-month withdrawal episode no longer becomes self-sustaining. The results demonstrate a procedure for approximating and evaluating LLM-generated decisions within a defined simulation environment; they do not establish that these responses represent the behaviour of bank managers or customers. JEL classification: C63, C72, G21, E43, G28
evidence_items.title: Estimating Decision Rules from Large Language Model Agents: An Application to Bank Balance-Sheet Management

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed academic research and institutional operations. Major LLMs, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, are now integrated into educational institutions at research and administrative levels. These LLMs go beyond summarizing text or polishing emails to include personalized learning, automated content creation, decision-making, and pedagogical integration. This chapter investigates the evolving role of LLMs in transforming the research landscape, particularly in academic writing, research management, pedagogy, evaluation, and ethical consideration. The research method is based on a systematic literature review (SLR) following PRISMA protocols, supported by bibliometric analysis and keyword-based thematic analysis of peer-reviewed articles from Web of Science and Scopus databases (2020–2025). Results revealed the existence of five major themes, namely academic writing and content generation, research evaluation, pedagogical integration, model comparison, and ethical considerations. The study highlights a sharp increase in publications since ChatGPT’s emergence, with thematic shifts toward education-related applications. Heatmaps across Scopus and WoS demonstrated significant trends toward real-world educational applications. However, ethical concerns showed strong growth, reflecting academic integrity issues. The keyword co-occurrence analysis also showed a dynamic research landscape with strong thematic ties to ethics, academic writing, teaching, and educational innovation. The overlay visualizations further illustrated the temporal evolution of topics from foundational concepts toward technology adoption, user experience, and collaborative learning. This chapter concludes by suggesting some recommendations to guide institutional policy and future research, ensuring an effective integration of LLMs in academic settings.
evidence_items.title: Transforming Research Management and Knowledge Creation With Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern marketing by integrating predictive analytics with generative creativity to enhance personalization, efficiency, and strategic decision-making. Predictive models enable data-driven insights through customer segmentation, demand forecasting, churn analysis, and campaign optimization, while generative AI introduces scalable content creation, automated design, and innovative product prototyping. Together, these technologies create intelligent marketing ecosystems capable of delivering real-time, context-aware experiences across diverse channels. However, challenges related to data quality, algorithmic bias, ethical concerns, privacy regulations, and system integration must be addressed to ensure responsible adoption. This chapter explores foundational AI techniques, key applications, creative advancements, and emerging research directions that shape the future of AI-driven marketing, emphasizing the need for transparent, ethical, and human-centric innovation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Marketing

evidence_items.summary: The penetration of artificial intelligence systems as general-purpose technologies into every aspect of social and economic life tests the adaptation capacity of legal systems to this dynamic process. This study analyses Türkiye's current position in AI governance and its future regulatory trajectory across three fundamental layers. First, although Türkiye does not yet have a stand-alone AI-specific statute, it evaluates how existing legal norms, such as the Law on the Protection of Personal Data, the Turkish Code of Obligations, and the Turkish Criminal Code, are applied to AI applications. Second, it posits that harmonisation with the EU AI Act (AIA) is not a mere policy choice but a commercial and technical necessity due to the Customs Union relationship between Türkiye and the EU. In this context, the nature of the AIA as a product safety instrument and its direct implications for Türkiye are examined. Third, the institutional transformation and the future AI governance landscape in Türkiye is addressed through the allocation of mandates between the newly established cybersecurity authority (SGB) and the Directorate General for National Technology and Artificial Intelligence (MTYZGM) under the Ministry of Industry and Technology. By providing a critical analysis of the recent legislative proposals submitted to the Turkish Grand National Assembly, the text emphasises the importance of Türkiye developing a unique regulatory strategy that fosters innovation while protecting fundamental rights. The study concludes that AI is not a transient hype but becoming a permanent and horizontal element of the Turkish legal framework.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Regulation in Türkiye: Current Position and Future Trajectory

evidence_items.summary: Background. Knowledge-graph models can rank existing drugs for a disease, but their benchmarks mostly reward rediscovering known treatments, and their scores rarely come with evidence a researcher can check. We built OREVID, an open tool that shows a ranked candidate only when an evidence line supports it and reports how often each line was right on held-out data, and compared it with TxGNN on identical data. Methods. The graph combines PrimeKG, Open Targets, STRING and PubTator3 (157,822 nodes, 9.46 million edges). For each disease, 22 degree-weighted metapath features feed a LightGBM LambdaRank model trained with masked neighbourhoods. A candidate is shown only if it is indicated for an ontology-neighbour disease or for a disease sharing at least 3 associated genes (hypergeometric p &lt; 10⁻⁵ over the genes with at least one associated disease). The acceptance criteria for these rules were set in advance; the rules were revised on the hidden-treatment benchmarks and then measured on an external set of approvals not used to choose them. TxGNN was retrained with its official code on the same PrimeKG splits, and all tasks and predictions are released as OREVID-bench. Results. Zero-shot Recall@100 (mean ± SD over five splits) was 0.811 ± 0.042 for OREVID, 0.412 ± 0.042 for TxGNN and 0.358 ± 0.040 for a popularity baseline, with OREVID ahead on every split (paired difference with TxGNN 0.399, 95% CI 0.352–0.443, resampling diseases). On nine disease areas held out it was 0.617 against 0.237, ahead in all nine, although TxGNN had the higher AUPRC in five. Training OREVID without validation labels and excluding diseases where TxGNN outputs constant scores gave 0.809 against 0.421.
evidence_items.title: OREVID: Open, Evidence-Based Drug Repurposing with a Benchmark Against TxGNN

evidence_items.summary: Using the UrbanSound8K dataset as a representative case, this study investigates how lightweight acoustic models can be trained with limited labeled data in resource-constrained environments. Because conventional knowledge distillation confines knowledge transfer to a single target dataset, it leaves the rich prior knowledge in external audio sources largely unused. We therefore propose Cross-DATA, a framework that treats a large-scale, general audio dataset such as FSD50K as an auxiliary knowledge source and integrates a newly designed Cross-data Attention Distillation mechanism. With mixed data batches as input, a powerful teacher model establishes inter-feature correlation patterns that the compact student network is encouraged to reproduce. In this way, the teacher's generic acoustic representations and discriminative capabilities can be transferred beyond the distribution of the target data, rather than being reduced to data augmentation or feature imitation. Experiments on UrbanSound8K show that the resulting student model surpasses traditional single-dataset distillation approaches in classification accuracy while using only about 4% of the teacher model's parameters and computational cost. Cross-DATA consequently alleviates the representational capacity deficit of lightweight models in small-data scenarios.
evidence_items.title: Cross-DATA: Cross-Data Attention Distillation for Lightweight Sound Classification with Limited Data

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents two related benchmark studies of AI-enabled wireless power transfer (WPT) for FR3 (7–24 GHz) ultra-massive MIMO (UM-MIMO) 6G base stations. Study 1 benchmarks time-slotted WPT scheduling across multiple IoT devices, comparing naive, sustainability-aware, round-robin and proportional-fair policies with a learned time-to-depletion predictor. Across 80 randomized 15-device populations, naive battery-priority scheduling saved none of the 238 physically sustainable devices, sustainability awareness raised the save rate to 23.5%, and a proportional-fair policy weighted by harvesting surplus performed best (51.7%), ahead of the learned predictor (42.4%). Study 2 asks whether an array should share its aperture between communication and WPT by partitioning its elements (power-splitting) or by alternating between the two functions in time (time-switching) under time-varying battery and queue demand. Power-splitting yielded shorter communication queues at every tested distance, and at 5 m, adaptive power-splitting avoided battery depletion in all 40 trials, whereas fixed allocation depleted the battery in every trial; adaptivity provided no such benefit under time-switching. Together, the studies indicate that the aperture-sharing architecture sets the achievable ceiling and the scheduling policy determines how close a deployment comes to it, so the architecture decision should be made first.
evidence_items.title: AI-Enabled Wireless Power Transfer for FR3 Ultra-Massive MIMO 6G Base Stations: A Multi-Device Scheduling and Aperture-Sharing Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Over the years, Uniform Resource Locator (URL) Phishing has been a threat to online security because their scams exploit trust in a misleading URL to trick unsuspecting users into disclosing their username or passwords and other personal information. Not only that, but it is also crucial to identify these malicious URLs and ensure online platforms and users are protected. The ISCXURL2016 data was utilized for the purpose of analyzing the performance of different Machine Learning (ML) models in differentiating phishing and legitimate URLs in this paper. A wide range of classifiers were explored including the classic classifiers as well as more advanced ensemble classifiers. The results of the experiments indicate that ensemble-based boosting models can be more beneficial for URL phishing detection. HistGradientBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 98.47%, followed closely by LightGBM and XGBoost that both outperformed the accuracy of 98%. The other classifiers, RandomForest and ExtraTrees, also performed well with accuracy above 97% and traditional classifiers such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) showed the poorest performance with an accuracy of 67.75%. The results show that the boosting-based ensembles provide a suitable negation of the complex and non-linear structure of phishing URLs. Along with empirical evaluation, it offers a Properties & Positioning viewpoint as well as the importance of the ML-based phishing detection in the broader context of cybersecurity issues. Moreover, it discusses the future directions, with Federated Learning (FL) in the context of decentralized and privacy-preserving collaboration and Large Language Models (LLM) in the context of semantic reasoning and flexibility. These insights together will provide the building blocks for more intelligent, adaptive and trustworthy phishing organizations.
evidence_items.title: Trustworthy Phishing URL Detection Using Machine Learning: Performance Analysis and Future Directions

evidence_items.summary: Fracture detection on musculoskeletal radiographs remains challenging, particularly when findings are subtle or visible on only one projection. This retrospective two-centre multi-reader diagnostic performance study evaluated an artificial intelligence system at the level of the complete radiographic examination and compared its performance with seven anonymized readers. Radiographic examinations from AGEL Šternberk Hospital and AGEL Vítkovice Hospital, acquired between 15 December 2025 and 25 January 2026, were retrospectively analysed. The primary endpoint was study-level fracture positivity, defined as at least one positive image within an examination; the same aggregation rule was applied to AI and reader assessments. Examinations of the spine, ribs, and hemithorax were excluded because these anatomies were outside the supported scope. The cohort comprised 526 examinations, including 101 fracture-positive and 425 fracture-negative studies. Sensitivity was 0.911 (95% CI, 0.839–0.952), specificity 0.899 (0.866–0.924), PPV 0.681 (0.599–0.754), NPV 0.977 (0.957–0.988), and accuracy 0.901 (0.873–0.924). Mean reader sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and accuracy were 0.853, 0.853, 0.598, 0.961, and 0.853, respectively. The AI showed higher point estimates than the mean of the seven readers across all principal diagnostic metrics. These findings support prospective evaluation of AI as a second-reader or workflow-support tool for fracture detection, particularly in examinations containing subtle or easily overlooked findings.
evidence_items.title: Study-Level Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence for Fracture Detection on Musculoskeletal Radiographs: A Retrospective Multi-Reader Study

evidence_items.summary:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human resource management (HRM), yet the cognitive and psychological factors associated with human resource (HR) professionals’ intentions to use AI remain incompletely understood. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and appraisal perspectives, this study examines the relative associations of Cognitive Evaluation, AI-Use Anxiety, AI-Related Job Insecurity, organizational AI use across HR functions, and AI Knowledge with behavioral intention to use AI. It also explores whether AI Knowledge moderates these relationships.
 
 
 
 Survey data were collected from 285 HR professionals. Confirmatory factor analyses assessed the measurement structure of the study constructs, followed by hierarchical moderated regression analyses examining their unique associations with behavioral intention and the exploratory moderating role of AI Knowledge.
 
 
 
 Cognitive Evaluation, reflecting perceived usefulness and ease of use, showed the strongest unique association with behavioral intention to use AI. AI-Use Anxiety demonstrated a smaller negative association, whereas AI-Related Job Insecurity, AI Use Across HR Functions, and AI Knowledge did not explain significant unique variance once the competing predictors were considered simultaneously. The comprehensive model explained 66.8% of the variance in behavioral intention. The exploratory interaction analyses provided no clear evidence that AI Knowledge systematically moderated the relationships examined.
 
 
 
 Organizations implementing AI in HR should address both employees’ evaluations of the technology and apprehension surrounding its use. Implementation strategies should demonstrate the practical usefulness and usability of AI through role-specific examples, hands-on training, and opportunities to experiment with AI tools in realistic HR contexts. Organizations should also recognize AI-use anxiety as a distinct potential barrier by providing accessible support, low-risk opportunities for familiarization, and clear communication throughout implementation. These strategies may help create conditions that support employees’ willingness to use AI.
 
 
 
 This study extends research on AI use intentions by examining cognitive, emotional, knowledge-related, and organizational-exposure factors simultaneously rather than in isolation. The findings show that HR professionals’ intentions to use AI are most strongly associated with evaluations of its usefulness and usability, while AI-use anxiety represents a smaller but distinct negative correlate. By distinguishing AI-use anxiety from AI-related job insecurity and individual AI knowledge from organizational AI exposure, the study provides a more differentiated account of the factors associated with HR professionals’ intentions to use AI.
evidence_items.title: Beyond usefulness: cognitive and emotional correlates of AI use intentions among HR professionals
