evidence_items.summary: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro
evidence_items.title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs

evidence_items.summary: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model's ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/
evidence_items.title: ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video Pretraining for Language-Conditioned Local Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in egocentric video understanding, but their ability to reason cooperatively from multiple embodied viewpoints remains largely unexplored. We study this problem through multi-robot cooperative dynamic spatial reasoning, where a model must answer spatial, temporal, visibility, and coordination questions by integrating synchronized egocentric videos from a team of moving robots. To support this setting, we introduce CoopSR, the first benchmark for this task, together with EgoTeam, a multi-robot egocentric QA dataset. EgoTeam contains 114,227 QA pairs spanning 19 question types, four difficulty tiers, and three team sizes in Habitat and iGibson, along with a real-world test set of around 2,326 QAs collected using two quadruped robots. We further propose SG-CoR (Spectral and Geometry-Aware Cooperative Reasoner), an MLLM framework for fine-grained cooperative spatial reasoning. SG-CoR combines dynamics-aware multi-robot frame sampling, spectral- and geometric-guided view fusion, and geometry- and motion-informed prompt distillation, enabling the model to benefit from privileged robot-pose supervision during training while requiring only egocentric videos at test time. Across 22 MLLM baselines, SG-CoR consistently improves cooperative reasoning, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned baseline by +3.87% on Habitat and +7.12% on iGibson. It also shows stronger generalization to unseen team sizes and real-world robot tests. Code can be found at https://github.com/KPeng9510/seeing-together.git.
evidence_items.title: Seeing Together: Multi-Robot Cooperative Egocentric Spatial Reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: The diagnosis of thyroid nodule cancers commonly utilizes ultrasound images. Several studies showed that deep learning algorithms designed to classify benign and malignant thyroid nodules could match radiologists' performance. However, data availability for training deep learning models is often limited due to the significant effort required to curate such datasets. Our previous study proposed a method (MADLaP) to curate thyroid nodule datasets automatically. It was tested to have a 63% yield rate and 83% accuracy. However, the usefulness of the generated data for training deep learning models remains unknown. In this study, we conducted experiments to determine whether using an automatically-curated dataset improves deep learning algorithms' performance. The expert annotations of 378 patients either trained a model directly (803 images) or built MADLaP, which curated 5,228 images from 3,981 patients; the same network and training method were used throughout, and 10-model cross-validation ensembles were tested on 378 nodules from an earlier period. The model trained on the automatically-curated dataset had a significantly higher AUC than the model trained on the manually selected dataset (0.657 vs 0.607; difference 0.051, 95% CI: 0.020, 0.081; P = .001), an advantage seen in all 22 configuration pairs. On the same test set, this model was within the AUC range of four radiologists (0.63-0.66) and not significantly different from a benchmark trained on 1,278 expert-curated nodules (0.69; difference -0.036, 95% CI: -0.083, 0.011), whereas manually curated models fell significantly below it. The Stage-1 subset (86% accuracy) did not differ significantly from the full MADLaP dataset (difference 0.015, 95% CI: -0.006, 0.036). In conclusion, we showed that using an automatically-curated dataset can substantially increase the performance of deep learning algorithms.
evidence_items.title: Effectiveness of Automatically Curated Dataset in Thyroid Nodules Classification Algorithms Using Deep Learning

evidence_items.summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler. Existing state files, PID locks, graceful shutdown, resume planning, manifest-key validation and the metric definitions remain supported. Manifest editor: structured forms, full YAML editing and effective-run previews share a common side-effect-free resolver with the CLI. New, duplicate, remove, reorder and Save As workflows preserve comments and quotes where supported. Saves show a diff and use atomic replacement with conflict detection; ambiguous YAML falls back to raw editing. Read-only mode and unsaved-change dialogs protect documents.

evidence_items.summary: We introduce  PhysAI  (“Fizzy”), an architecture for situated physical judgement: deciding what action is  appropriate from  incomplete evidence, relevant experience, physical predictions, competing goals, and capabilities on which an agent can rely. The agent works with a provisional account of what the physical situation is doing and revises it as observations, outcomes, priorities, and available capabilities change.  It  is distinguished from  contemporary forms of AI agents by the extent  to  which it  applies judgement to decide which  physical  factors apply to a  given context ,  and its ability to  update its beliefs and provide a professional account of itself .    PhysAI  is built around three proposed additions: world models for physical inference and prediction, self-adapting subagents, and a capability register grounding expectations of ability. Reasonin g models  and the  agent   harness  support their interaction.   Physical work often requires action before information is complete, and both the basis for a decision and its appropriateness can change. Later observations  remain  partial evidence. A prediction may remain  accurate  while the action it supported becomes inappropriate because priorities, commitments, authority, or alternatives have changed.   Four domain cases illustrate the architecture  and added value . The research agenda tests the individual and combined contribution of the three proposed additions to  timely ,  appropriate decisions , including cases in which seeking more information consumes time while the physical process continues.
evidence_items.title: PhysAI: An architecture for situated physical judgement

evidence_items.summary: Intelligent question answering for textile standards requires accurate domain understanding, clause retrieval, and evidence-grounded generation, yet general-purpose large language models often lack sufficient domain adaptation and factual support. This study proposes a textile-standard question-answering framework that integrates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning with multidimensional retrieval-augmented generation (MDRAG). Based on 7017 domestic and international textile standards, we constructed a structured knowledge resource containing 121,166 annotated domain elements and a task-specific dataset of 2000 question–answer pairs. Qwen3.5-9B-Base, Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, and GLM-4-9B were evaluated under three primary settings: Baseline, Baseline+LoRA, and Baseline+LoRA+MDRAG. A separate comparison with conventional RAG was conducted to assess the additional benefit of multidimensional retrieval over single-path retrieval. Among the primary settings, Qwen3.5-9B-Base with LoRA+MDRAG achieved the highest overall performance, with a cosine similarity of 0.624, a BLEU score of 0.283, and an expert-based overall score of 24.4. These findings support the use of lightweight domain adaptation together with multidimensional structured knowledge retrieval for textile-standard question answering.
evidence_items.title: A Textile Standardization Large Language Model Integrating LoRA Fine-Tuning and Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can render structured questionnaire variables as natural-language profiles, but their value in mental-health screening cannot be judged from a single fixed-threshold score. We evaluated LLM prompt conditions in a cross-questionnaire benchmark for predicting screen-positive status on the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) among undergraduates. The intended application was an offline methodological benchmark using previously collected questionnaire data, not a shorter alternative to direct SDS administration. Methods De-identified records were assigned to Development (n=1,951), Test (n=2,186), and Holdout (n=2,258) grade cohorts. We evaluated logistic regression, XGBoost, and 12 model-prompt conditions at the fixed 0.5 threshold and at thresholds selected only in Development-validation. We also examined paired bootstrap differences, ranking stability, scale correlations, grouped ablations, cohort shift, calibration intercepts and slopes, alternative expected calibration error specifications, representative repeated calls at temperatures 0 and 0.1, sex-stratified performance, and per-1,000 screening scenarios. Results At the fixed 0.5 threshold on Test, GPT E1, Gemini E2, and XGBoost achieved macro-F1 values of 0.732, 0.730, and 0.674. At Development-derived thresholds of 0.38, 0.50, and 0.174, the corresponding macro-F1 values were 0.702, 0.730, and 0.660. At the Development-selected specificity target, XGBoost achieved a Test macro-F1 of 0.738. Pairwise intervals showed no clear fixed-0.5 macro-F1 difference among the three highest-ranked LLM conditions. XGBoost yielded the lowest Brier scores. The combined-sample Spearman correlation between SDS and SAS was 0.60. Together with the ablation results, this correlation indicated predictive information distributed across overlapping questionnaire groups rather than dependence on a single measured group.
evidence_items.title: SDS screen-positive prediction from structured questionnaires in university students: a comparative evaluation of large language model prompting strategies

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into clinical decision support, ranging from documentation aids to triage and patient communication. However, their behavior in ethically ambiguous medical situations is poorly characterized. Variability in how different LLMs balance approval of against refusal of a proposed action could materially shape the recommendations clinicians receive, yet no widely shared benchmark systematically quantifies this variability across contemporary model families. Objective This study aimed to develop a standardized case-based audit set of medical ethics dilemmas and quantify variation in recommendation direction, model-reported confidence, within-model stability, and between-model agreement across 5 selected contemporary LLMs. Methods We constructed 60 original medical ethics dilemmas spanning 4 domains. Three researchers independently annotated case difficulty and ethical principles before reaching consensus. Five primary models—GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, full-size DeepSeek-R1, and Meta Llama-3-8B-Instruct—were each evaluated 3 times per case using a fixed prompt and temperature 0. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B was evaluated separately as an exploratory small-model comparator. The primary outcome was the binary yes or no answer; model-reported confidence and reason were also collected. Model differences were assessed using a case-clustered generalized estimating equation (GEE), and between-model agreement and within-model stability were summarized. Results Of 900 planned primary panel outputs, 897 (99.7%) had valid binary answers. Trial-level yes rates were 44.4% (80/180) for DeepSeek-R1, 42.4% (75/177) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, 38.9% (70/180) for GPT-5, 38.9% (70/180) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 16.7% (30/180) for Llama-3-8B. The overall model effect was significant (Wald χ24=23.34; P<.001); after Holm adjustment, only comparisons involving Llama-3-8B were significant.
evidence_items.title: Variation in Medical Ethics Recommendations Across Large Language Models: Case-Based Audit Study

evidence_items.summary: Brazilian public-safety agencies release structured crime statistics but withhold the free-text narrative field of police reports, which is rich in modus operandi and contextual information, because it contains personal data protected by the Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD). We address this deadlock for robbery reports with a fully local (on-premise) two-stage anonymization pipeline: a deterministic regular-expression stage for structured personally identifiable information (PII) and a pluggable semantic layer (dedicated NER, local LLMs served by Ollama, union and chained hybrids, and Microsoft Presidio as a system baseline). We contribute (i) an expert-annotated gold standard of 996 robbery narratives, released with the source code; (ii) an entity-level evaluation protocol whose headline metric is safety recall (how much PII actually did not leak), complemented by a re-identification-criticality analysis and bootstrap confidence intervals; and (iii) an empirical benchmark of nine engine configurations quantifying the safety–utility trade-off. The union of spaCy and qwen3:8b over the regex stage reaches the highest macro safety recall (0.986, 95% CI [0.972; 0.994]; micro 0.973) and is the most conservative (highest-recall) option, while qwen3:8b alone gives the best overall balance (safety recall 0.966, precision 0.80, micro-F1 0.826, text retention 96%) and is our recommendation for general use. In this configuration, direct identifiers (names, documents, phones, e-mails) are removed at 99–100%, with residual leakage concentrated in location quasi-identifiers. Safety recall measures PII removal, not residual reidentification risk: these figures bound leakage rather than certify anonymity. We recommend qwen3:8b for general supervised anonymization, and the union when leakage must be minimized, and discuss conditions for replication across Brazilian police forces.
evidence_items.title: Local Anonymization of Free-Text Robbery Police Reports in Brazilian Portuguese: a Safety-Recall-Oriented Multi-Model Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Lithium–sulfur cycle life is limited by dissolved LiyS q x polysulfides whose speciation remains disputed. We benchmark the complete matrix (y = 0–2, q = 0 to −2, x = 1–8) in the gas phase, tetraglyme and dimethyl sulfoxide: 248 M06-2X/SMD thermochemistries, 132 refined by single-point CCSD. The convex hull, S8 → Li2S6 → Li2S4 → Li2S3 → Li2S2 → Li2S, is identical in both solvents, and every exergonic long-chain comproportionation delivers Li2S6. QTAIM analysis of the CCSD densities separates covalent S–S from electrostatic Li–S bonding, transferably between solvents. Solvation makes S 2–x the dominant lithium-free 1 charge state and places both legs of the shuttle on that branch. Infrared and Raman spectra of prepared solutions test the vibrational predictions and track the chain-length distribution through one band envelope. The open dataset is a calibrated reference for force-field, machine-learned and continuum battery models.
evidence_items.title: Lithium Polysulfide Speciation in Lithium–Sulfur Batteries: A First-Principles Benchmark of Thermodynamics, Bonding, and Solvent Control

evidence_items.summary: Financial derivatives occupy a core position in modern asset allocation, but the traditional option pricing framework, particularly the Black-Scholes (B-S) model, faces unprecedented challenges when applied to the highly volatile cryptocurrency market. The B-S assumption of constant volatility and continuous price paths fundamentally fails to capture the volatility smile, heavy-tailed distributions, and intermittent crashes inherent in digital assets. Furthermore, structural frictions such as liquidity fragmentation render the crypto ecosystem an incomplete market. This paper systematically reviews the mathematical transition from the B-S framework to high-order stochastic processes, specifically the Heston and Jump-Diffusion models. Most importantly, we contribute to the existing literature by providing a rigorous empirical evaluation using out-of-sample high-frequency options data from Deribit. Our empirical results quantitatively confirm the theoretical limitations of traditional pricing: while the Heston model reduces the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) by approximately 45%, the Stochastic Volatility with Jumps (SVJ) model demonstrates absolute superiority in pricing tail risks. Specifically, the SVJ framework decreases the valuation error for deep out-of-the-money (OTM) options by over 72% compared to the baseline B-S model. Ultimately, this study emphasizes that structurally integrating both continuous volatility clustering and discrete market shocks is mathematically indispensable for robust risk management in decentralized financial markets.
evidence_items.title: Valuation Engines Under Market Incompleteness: An Empirical Benchmark of High-Order Option Pricing in Digital Asset Markets

evidence_items.summary: Automatic auscultation is usually evaluated on the ICBHI 2017 database, where published scores depend on the split and the metric adopted. This work measures what a deployable model reaches under a fixed protocol: the official split, five seeds, patient-level bootstrap intervals, and an equivalence margin fixed in advance. Six configurations are compared, a compact convolutional neural network (CNN) trained from scratch, a closed-form continuous-time (CfC) recurrent network, and two pretrained models, MobileNetV3 on ImageNet and PANNs CNN6 on AudioSet. The compact CNN (556 500 parameters) obtains an ICBHI score of 0.460±0.017 and a binary area under the curve (AUC) of 0.572, with a patient-level interval of [0.515,0.630]. No pretrained configuration discriminates detectably better, and equivalence within the margin holds only between the CNN and its 8-bit integer (INT8) version. That level needs its baselines: a classifier that always predicts Normal scores 0.500, above every trained configuration, and an audio-free indicator of the recording device reaches an AUC of 0.582. The discrimination of the CNN ranges from 0.627 on the most represented device to 0.468 on the least, and the CfC stays at chance, which irregular event timing does not change. Quantized to INT8 with the classifier in floating point, the CNN occupies 0.58 MB and runs in 30.4 ms per cycle on a Raspberry Pi 5 without thermal throttling. Replacing the official score by a per-class macro average raises the figure by 0.121 to 0.183 on the same predictions.
evidence_items.title: A Reproducible Benchmark of Compact, Pretrained, and Continuous-Time Models for Respiratory Sound Classification at the Edge

evidence_items.summary: Gold Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) provide investors with exposure to gold prices without requiring direct ownership of physical gold. Differences in fund expenses, benchmark replication and other operational factors may cause individual ETFs to perform differently. This study evaluates five selected Gold ETFs in India—Kotak, SBI, Nippon India, HDFC and Axis—over the period from 1 April 2021 to 30 March 2026. The analysis uses daily net asset values (NAVs), a domestic Indian gold-price series denominated in Indian rupees, and Nifty 50 index values. The analytical framework includes cumulative returns, compound annual growth rate (CAGR), annualised volatility, the Sharpe ratio, correlation, regression and tracking-error analysis. Three hypotheses are tested using the Friedman test, Newey–West heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) tests of mean active returns, and HAC-robust regression analysis. The domestic gold-price series generated a cumulative return of 232.19%, compared with 208.10%–216.46% for the five ETFs and 52.01% for the Nifty 50 price index. Kotak recorded the highest cumulative return among the five ETFs, the highest Sharpe ratio and the lowest tracking error. The Friedman test identified statistically significant differences in daily-return rankings among the ETFs. After Holm adjustment, Kotak exhibited statistically significant negative mean daily active returns relative to gold, whereas the corresponding results for the other four ETFs were not statistically significant. HAC-robust regressions also indicated significant positive relationships between each ETF's returns and gold-price returns. The findings demonstrate that absolute returns, risk-adjusted performance and tracking efficiency represent distinct dimensions of Gold ETF performance. Keywords: Gold ETFs, NAV, risk–return analysis, Sharpe ratio, tracking error, domestic gold prices, Nifty 50, hypothesis testing.
evidence_items.title: Performance, Risk and Benchmark Tracking of Selected Gold ETFs in India: A Comparative Study with Domestic Gold Prices and the Nifty 50 (2021–2026)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Individual‐tree segmentation from three‐dimensional forest point clouds underpins forest inventory, biomass estimation and ecosystem monitoring, but remains challenging in structurally complex stands, where vertical heterogeneity and point‐density degradation weaken the robustness of centre‐offset‐based instance grouping. We present TreeSegAgent, an extensible framework for forest point‐cloud analysis, whose core segmentation component is a multi‐anchor framework for tree segmentation (MA‐TreeSeg). MA‐TreeSeg stabilizes instance formation through two modules. First, a multi‐anchor (three‐vertical‐anchor) structural grouping module within an enhanced PointGroup‐style instance segmentation network, explicitly encoding tree vertical structure to improve grouping stability under sparse canopy conditions and to better recover low‐stature and understory trees. Second, we incorporate segment anything model (SAM)‐driven trunk constraint module. SAM is applied on two‐dimensional projections to identify trunk regions and generate trunk candidates, which are then employed as spatial hard constraints to regularize centre‐offset predictions and suppress clustering drift under canopy overlap. To support reproducible ecological workflow, TreeSegAgent further provides a task‐driven agent for automated, specification‐driven orchestration of common point‐cloud operations (e.g. instance segmentation, DEM generation and height‐based filtering) across datasets. Across multiple forest point‐cloud benchmarks, our method yields more spatially coherent individual‐tree instances and improved robustness to density variation, offering an extensible solution for large‐scale forest point‐cloud analysis.
evidence_items.title:
<scp>TreeSegAgent</scp>
                    : Agentic tree instance segmentation via a multi‐anchor pipeline

evidence_items.summary: This study evaluates how LLMs interpret Words of Estimative Probability (WEPs) in Brazilian Portuguese compared to English. We translated an English benchmark and compared multilingual models (GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Flash) against a region-specific model (Sabiá 4). Our findings reveal a “tail smoothing” phenomenon, where models systematically compress extreme probabilities. Notably, while Gemini 3 Flash demonstrated remarkable cross-lingual stability, GPT-5.1 exhibited significant calibration degradation. Counterintuitively, when measured against the English human baseline, Sabiá 4 displayed the most aggressive distribution compression. These results suggest a complex dynamic: either linguistic fine-tuning does not ensure alignment, or it actively captures a culturally specific pragmatic ambiguity in Brazilian Portuguese. This exposes the vulnerabilities and nuances of deploying deploying LLMs in nuanced semantic tasks in Brazilian Portuguese.
evidence_items.title: Tail Smoothing and Cross-Lingual Volatility: Evaluating Estimative Uncertainty in Large Language Models for Brazilian Portuguese

evidence_items.summary: Natural Language to Structured Query Language (NL2SQL) systems have advanced with large language models (LLMs), yet evaluations remain centered on English, leaving open how these systems behave across languages and language varieties. We aim to contribute to this by analyzing two state-of-the-art LLMs (LLaMA 3.3 70B and Qwen 3.6 35B, both zero-shot) on the WikiSQL benchmark in English, Brazilian Portuguese (PT-BR), and European Portuguese (PT-PT), keeping database schemas and inference configuration fixed. Translations were validated through distance metrics (cosine similarity 0.966), contrastive linguistic analysis confirming varietal features (e.g., cleft constructions 36.8× more frequent in PT-PT), and multi-model judgment (85% / 81% semantic equivalence, 95.5% PT-BR and 96.0% PT-PT inter-judge agreement). Results show a marked drop from English (47.25% EX) to Portuguese (PT-BR: 40.03%; PT-PT: 39.34%), with the PT-BR vs. PT-PT difference reaching statistical significance (p = 0.019). English-only successes outnumber Portuguese-only successes nearly 10:1. A replication on a second model (Qwen 3.6 35B) confirms the English-Portuguese gap but suggests that intralinguistic effects may be model-dependent. Stratified analyses show semantic complexity and quantification amplify degradation, particularly for COUNT queries. These findings point to persistent English bias in NL2SQL and measurable effects of intralinguistic variation, even between closely related varieties.
evidence_items.title: The Impact of Language and Portuguese Intralinguistic Variation on NL2SQL

evidence_items.summary: The use of textbooks as primary sources of information has increasingly given way to tools based on Large Language Models (LLMs), raising concerns about the reliability of generated answers. This study investigates how different adaptation strategies shape the behavior of small language models in educational Question Answering (QA) tasks in Portuguese. To support this analysis, we built a question-answer dataset derived from an NLP textbook and compared base models and the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline with models adapted through supervised fine-tuning and Continued Pretraining. The evaluation relies on questions from the LARI dataset, which has been validated by human specialists, and combines automatic and qualitative assessment procedures. The findings indicate that small models tuned with structured instructional knowledge achieve stronger semantic alignment and produce more pertinent answers in Portuguese educational QA scenarios.
evidence_items.title: Textbook-Enriched Training for Language Models: Boosting Answer Quality in Specialized Contexts

evidence_items.summary: Ableism is a form of discrimination directed at people with disabilities that can appear through explicit offenses, but also through subtle, indirect, and context-dependent expressions that are difficult to identify automatically. This challenge remains underexplored in content moderation, particularly in Brazilian Portuguese. This paper investigates how different levels of prompt information affect the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in detecting ableist comments on social media. To this end, we build a dataset from YouTube comments related to disability-related content, followed by manual annotation. Four LLMs are evaluated using five progressively detailed prompts, ranging from a simple classification instruction to prompts that include definitions, examples, contextual information, and the video transcript. Results show that more informative prompts tend to improve classification performance, although the effect varies across models. Qualitative inspection further reveals that LLMs often struggle to distinguish ableist discourse from criticism of ableism, as well as to separate ableism from other forms of offensive or discriminatory language. These findings highlight the importance of contextualized prompting for sensitive classification tasks and point to the need for further research on ableism detection in Portuguese.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Toxicity: Evaluating Language Models for Ableism Detection in Online Social Media

evidence_items.summary: O uso de Large Language Models (LLMs) em sistemas agênticos locais enfrenta desafios críticos de consistência e confiabilidade, especialmente em hardware de consumo. Este trabalho apresenta o protocolo STAB, uma metodologia de avaliação em escada de complexidade (S1→S4) combinada a um protocolo de estabilidade temporal para diagnosticar falhas em agentes on-premise. Avaliamos oito modelos de quatro famílias (Qwen, Gemma, Llama e Mistral) em servidor com GPU NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12 GB VRAM). Os resultados revelam que as falhas agênticas originam-se predominantemente na camada de instrução e decisão contextual, e não na capacidade bruta dos modelos. Identificamos o fenômeno de tool-skipping por nomeação semântica (H12) e demonstramos que conformidade de formato e acurácia semântica são dimensões ortogonais (H10). O modelo gemma4:e4b destacou-se como referência de maior confiabilidade, mantendo desempenho perfeito em todos os níveis de complexidade.
evidence_items.title: STAB: A Complexity-Ladder Framework for Evaluating Local LLMs as Autonomous Agents

evidence_items.summary: Spam over Internet Telephony (SPIT) detection faces escalating adversarial evasion via behavioral mimicry, while deep learning defenses often struggle to meet real-time scalability and transparency requirements. We formalize the “Fraudster’s Trilemma” and evaluate lightweight classifiers over an eight-dimensional feature space spanning physical, volumetric, and behavioral planes, using a simulation of 500,000 subscriber profiles across three stages of adversarial complexity (E1–E3). Ablation evidence indicates that the behavioral vector collapses under calibrated mimicry (F0.5 = 0.03 under Random Forest at E3), while the infrastructure-bound physical vector sustains an independent boundary of F0.5 = 0.98; the volumetric vector collapses under a linear boundary but persists under tree ensembles, which recover the class boundary from dispersion statistics that this benchmark does not equalize. Lightweight ensembles sustain high precision on this benchmark while scoring each subscriber independently, and per-decision SHAP attributions give operators an auditable justification for each blocking decision.
evidence_items.title: Lightweight SPIT Detection Under Adversarial Mimicry

organizations: Cleveland Clinic Lerner College of Medicine
evidence_items.summary: This repository provides the heart-sound recordings and respiratory noise needed to reproduce the cross-cohort data augmentation experiments for an Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) heart murmur detection model. The SQLite database contains recordings and murmur labels from four cohorts: CirCor DigiScope (PhysioNet 2022), used for training and validation, and WC2023, WVU, and OHH-2025, used only for external evaluation. The accompanying archive contains 174 respiratory recordings from the ICBHI 2017 database, which the training code mixes into heart sounds on the fly as noise augmentation.
evidence_items.title: Dataset to Reproduce: Systematic Evaluation of Data Augmentation Strategies for Cross-Cohort Heart Murmur Detection

evidence_items.summary: General-purpose LLMs asked to output a structured AI-ness verdict can serve as text detectors at near-zero cost, and their availability is governed less by model quality than by the free-tier policies of the gateways that serve them. This report benchmarks 20+ models across four gateways (OpenRouter free pool, NVIDIA NIM free tier, Google AI Studio free tier, and a local multi-account router) on a 48-text in-sample corpus and a 48-text disjoint holdout drawn from HC3, all scored through the same strict-JSON prompt, a fixed decision band (AI >= 0.69, HUMAN = 0.60). Three findings stand out. First, model choice dominates tuning: identical prompts and parsers span 0.31 to 1.00 corpus accuracy. Second, each gateway enforces a materially different regime -- OpenRouter has two 429 classes that require opposite remedies, Google's per-model daily quota (nominally 20) delivers a volume that is per model and per project (5-46 requests in one window observed) and stacks linearly with extra project keys, and NVIDIA free serving windows open and close within hours -- so a free model's measured accuracy and its usability as a live lane are separate, per-gateway questions. Third, in-sample perfection does not transfer: a lane that erred zero times on the corpus its band was fitted on produced a false negative out of sample. Part II (window 2026-10-13 to 2026-10-17) adds four findings and one retraction. (1) Accuracy does not survive listing: the lane Part I ranked first was delisted by its gateway four days after its window closed (HTTP 410, permanent), and another advertised model answers 404 on every real call while still appearing in GET /v1/models -- so availability must be probed per model, per gateway, on the day of use, and a catalogue listing is not a health check.
evidence_items.title: Free-Tier LLM Gateways as AI-Text Detectors: A Dated Benchmark of Model Accuracy, Quota Regimes, Availability Churn and Out-of-Sample Stability

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains supplementary computational data, MATLAB programs, and numerical results supporting the research manuscript entitled "Modelling and analysis of diphtheria transmission incorporating vaccination, asymptomatic carriage, environmental contamination, optimal control and model-based intervention efficiency", authored by Timothy Terfa Ashezua, Reuben Iortyer Gweryina, and Meshack Ogbaji, Department of Mathematics, Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University, Makurdi, Nigeria. The study formulates and analyses a deterministic nine-compartment diphtheria transmission model incorporating imperfect vaccination, breakthrough infections, asymptomatic carriage, treatment and isolation, waning immunity, and environmental contamination. The mathematical analysis investigates positivity, boundedness, disease-free and endemic equilibria, the basic reproduction number, stability, bifurcation, sensitivity, vaccination thresholds, and optimal intervention strategies. The supplementary materials include: MATLAB programs: Computational scripts for numerical simulations, sensitivity analysis, equilibrium calculations, and optimal-control investigations. Sensitivity analysis datasets: A Latin hypercube sampling dataset consisting of 5,000 samples across 27 model parameters, together with 500 bootstrap resampling index sets and partial rank correlation coefficient (PRCC) results. Numerical simulation results: Model-generated trajectories illustrating baseline transmission dynamics and the effects of vaccination, detection and treatment, sanitation, and combined interventions. Optimal-control results: State, adjoint, and control trajectories for intervention strategies involving vaccination/boosting, carrier screening, treatment/isolation, and environmental decontamination. Convergence and reproducibility data: Forward–backward sweep iteration logs, numerical convergence diagnostics, and grid-refinement comparisons.
evidence_items.title: Computational Data and MATLAB Codes for a Diphtheria Transmission Model Incorporating Vaccination, Asymptomatic Carriage, Environmental Contamination and Optimal Control

evidence_items.summary: This article presents an analytical-DES benchmark for intra-aisle robotic picking in automated warehousing. The investigated cycle combines horizontal shuttle travel, tote handling and item picking at storage locations. Simulation results are compared with the analytical formulation of Lerher et al. under the same rack geometry, shuttle-motion, handling and picking conditions, and the same definitions of cycle time and derived item throughput. Reproducing the published analytical tables requires the distance interpretation dES = 1.5 m and dTB = 0 m. The analytical-DES benchmark comprises 180 scenarios formed from three rack lengths, two paired motion profiles and n = 1 to 30 visited picking locations, with ten simulation replications per scenario. The six n = 1 cases are reported separately because no travel-between component is present. Across the remaining 174 scenarios, the mean absolute relative cycle-time discrepancy is 0.8655%, the median is 0.6758%, and the maximum is 7.0370%. The mean absolute error is 2.411 s and the RMSE is 2.744 s. The simulated scenario-mean cycle time is below the analytical value in all 174 principal scenarios. The results therefore show close numerical correspondence under the tested conditions, but not exact agreement, formal statistical equivalence, or validation against an operating warehouse.
evidence_items.title: Reconstruction and Discrete-Event Simulation Assessment of an Analytical

evidence_items.summary: Contextual integrity (CI) holds that the appropriateness of sharing personal information depends on the context of the information flow, not on the information alone. However, existing CI benchmarks often use independent scenarios that vary multiple CI parameters simultaneously and are dominated by inappropriate flows, making it unclear whether correct predictions reflect sensitivity to context or a general refusal tendency. We present ConCI, a controlled-counterfactual benchmark in which an anchor flow is paired with two counterfactuals that each modify a single CI parameter. The resulting triplet is scored jointly, with credit given only when all three flows are judged correctly. Built from six existing benchmarks, ConCI contains 1,592 flows in 556 triplets, is approximately label-balanced, and is validated by seven human annotators per flow. Across seven LLMs, many correct anchor predictions fail on at least one counterfactual, and even the strongest model errs on about a fifth of triplets. Furthermore, models perform near ceiling on inappropriate flows but weaker on appropriate ones, often continuing to judge a flow inappropriate even when a contextual change should make it appropriate. Larger models narrow this bias toward non-disclosure but do not eliminate it, and reasoning yields only modest gains.
evidence_items.title: ConCI: A Controlled Counterfactual Benchmark for Contextual Integrity in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Time-dependent routing recognizes that the same journey can take a different time depending on when it begins. Under duration minimization, even the departure time of each vehicle becomes a decision. Exact methods for this setting exist in the literature, but researchers and practitioners have lacked a ready-to-use open solver that combines rich piecewise-linear travel times, early feasible solutions and optimality claims. KAYROS fills this gap with two modes on one checker-consistent engine: an Iterated Local Search that streams improving solutions and a Branch-Price-and-Cut method that can issue computational optimality certificates under explicit arithmetic and search assumptions. It installs with one command and has no proprietary dependency. The public MAMUT-routing store currently contains 704 KAYROS certificates under a four-solve publication protocol, which has also led to the retraction and repair of invalid earlier claims. The report presents two complementary benchmark contributions to MAMUT-routing. The first integrates Blauth2024, a benchmark from the literature whose travel times derive from measured Uber speeds, for which KAYROS provides new best-known solutions on all 40 instances. The second proposes Poryos2026, a new benchmark of 1,080 paired static and time-dependent instances built from OpenStreetMap road networks and controlled synthetic traffic. Finally, the report describes the intensive human-AI collaboration behind this work and the verification practices that kept its outputs independently verifiable.
evidence_items.title: KAYROS: An Anytime and Exact Open-Source Solver for Duration-Minimization Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing. A Technical Report and a Case Study in Human-AI Engineering

evidence_items.summary: Natural language messages often contain quasi-identifiers that are weak in isolation but can jointly reveal an individual's private attributes. We call such a jointly revealing set of cues a quasi-evidence group. Existing privacy benchmarks focus on explicit identifiers, attribute inference, or task-driven disclosures, leaving inference from quasi-evidence groups largely unmeasured. In practice, whether exposing such a quasi-evidence group violates privacy also depends on sender-specified disclosure policies. We introduce QuasiLeak-Bench, a benchmark for policy-conditioned quasi-evidence group recovery, which evaluates whether detectors recover complete quasi-evidence groups and flag the disclosures the given policy prohibits. To obtain reliable ground truth at scale, a reverse-construction pipeline first selects weak quasi-identifiers, composes them into quasi-evidence groups verified to jointly reveal a target attribute, and generates documents around this evidence, followed by automated quality control. Experiments show that existing privacy detectors transfer poorly to QuasiLeak-Bench, and locally deployable LLM-based detectors fall far behind proprietary models, mainly because they miss most quasi-evidence groups altogether. However, a 4B model fine-tuned on our training split surpasses the strongest prompted model on held-out documents, showing that the task is learnable.
evidence_items.title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery

evidence_items.summary: Low-light video processing remains an underexplored problem in computer vision, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality ground-truth data. Existing public datasets exhibit several limitations, including restricted motion diversity, limited scene coverage, weak degradations, reliance on auxiliary modalities such as event data, and misalignment between low-light inputs and ground truth. Furthermore, current datasets typically address either low-light enhancement or scene understanding, whereas these tasks should be considered jointly. We introduce \textbf{OLiVES}, a benchmark dataset for outdoor low-light videos with dynamic scenes, designed to support both low-light video enhancement (LLVE) and video object segmentation (VOS). The dataset addresses key content gaps by incorporating a diverse range of natural textures, animals, occlusions, dynamic activities, and close-up scenes. To the best of our knowledge, OLiVES is the first outdoor low-light video dataset captured using professional cinema-grade cameras. It provides over 25,000 aligned normal- and low-light frame pairs, along with over 46,000 VOS annotations. We benchmark state-of-the-art LLVE and VOS methods on OLiVES and show that training on it improves performance on both tasks. The OLiVES project page is available at: https://anonymous-OLiVES.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: OLiVES: An Outdoor Low-Light Video Benchmark for Enhancement and Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.
evidence_items.title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to support long-horizon reasoning and decision making. Existing memory systems typically retrieve historical trajectories or summaries as independent context fragments, overlooking the procedural dependencies underlying multi-step execution. As memory scales, such flat retrieval introduces context fragmentation and cross-task interference, leading to structurally inconsistent reasoning trajectories. We propose ActiveMem, a hierarchical memory framework that recursively organizes agent experiences into dependency-aware latent execution trees. ActiveMem abstracts trajectories into reusable subtask nodes while explicitly preserving execution transitions, enabling coherent reasoning-path retrieval conditioned on the current execution state. To support continual adaptation, ActiveMem further learns dynamic memory expansion, retrieval, and pruning policies through reinforcement learning. Experiments across various agent benchmarks demonstrate that ActiveMem consistently improves task completion, reasoning stability, and memory efficiency over existing memory-based agents. Moreover, ActiveMem enables compact open-weight models to achieve competitive performance with substantially larger proprietary systems.
evidence_items.title: ActiveMem: Dynamic Latent Memory Trees for Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large video models have exhibited impressive performance on a wide range of visual question answering tasks, owing to the rise of powerful, pretrained text and vision encoders. The usefulness of such models have also been demonstrated on a wide range of benchmarks, with an important caveat - the dominant approach in these benchmarks evaluates multiple choice reasoning via text options. This is a natural way to test text-based reasoning in these models, and has led to significant insights regarding model behavior in the community. In this work, we ask a different question - what happens when the evaluation modality is visual, rather than text? We introduce three new vision-centric evaluation benchmarks in temporal frame retrieval, video future prediction, and causal memory distortion, all designed around evaluating visual understanding capabilities in large video models. Our approach complements the existing approaches to evaluate video understanding in frontier models. We show that current frontier models exhibit significant weakness when attempting to reason through visual queries, rather than text. We conclude with an extended analysis section that provides pointers for future improvements in visual understanding for large video models.
evidence_items.title: Not Another Text Benchmark: Putting the "Visual" Back in Visual Question Answering for Large Video Models

evidence_items.summary: Video misinformation increasingly operates at the semantic and evidential level: authentic footage may be selectively edited, temporally reordered, spliced across sources, or augmented with AI-generated content to construct false narratives. Such evidence-dependent manipulations cannot be reliably verified from the input video alone, because the missing, reordered, replaced, or recontextualized evidence lies outside the video itself. We introduce \textbf{EVID-Bench}, a benchmark for search-grounded video misinformation detection, where a system must search the open web for related videos and identify what information is false through cross-video comparison. EVID-Bench comprises 222 videos spanning 9 manipulation types across 3 categories: AI generation, single-source editing, and multi-source editing. All samples are verified to be undetectable by frontier models through visual inspection alone. We evaluate nine frontier multimodal models using a retrieval-augmented verification baseline. The best system achieves only 61.43\% point-level accuracy and 43.24\% video-level accuracy, while AI-generated manipulations remain especially challenging. Error analysis reveals recurring challenges: models fixate on irrelevant anchors, misattribute synthetic content to editorial splicing, and terminate search prematurely before fully explaining the manipulation.
evidence_items.title: When Seeing Is Not Believing -- A Benchmark for Search-Grounded Video Misinformation Detection

evidence_items.summary: Most existing hyperspectral image super-resolution methods require modifications for different scales, limiting their flexibility in arbitrary-scale reconstruction. 2D Gaussian splatting provides a continuous representation that is compatible with arbitrary-scale super-resolution. Existing methods often rely on rasterization strategies, which may limit flexible spatial modeling. Extending them to hyperspectral image super-resolution remains challenging, as the task requires adaptive spatial reconstruction while preserving spectral fidelity. This paper proposes GaussianHSI, a Gaussian-Splatting-based framework for arbitrary-scale hyperspectral image super-resolution. We develop a Voronoi-Guided Bilateral 2D Gaussian Splatting for spatial reconstruction. After predicting a set of Gaussian functions to represent the input, it associates each target pixel with relevant Gaussian functions through Voronoi-guided selection. The target pixel is then reconstructed by aggregating the selected Gaussian functions with reference-aware bilateral weighting, which considers both geometric relevance and consistency with low-resolution features. We further introduce a Spectral Detail Enhancement module to improve spectral reconstruction. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of GaussianHSI over state-of-the-art methods for arbitrary-scale hyperspectral image super-resolution.
evidence_items.title: Voronoi-guided Bilateral 2D Gaussian Splatting for Arbitrary-Scale Hyperspectral Image Super-Resolution

evidence_items.summary: Assuming that neither source data nor source model parameters are accessible, black-box domain adaptation (BBDA) represents a highly practical yet challenging setting, where transferable knowledge is limited to the predictions of a black-box source model. Existing approaches exploit such knowledge via pseudo-label refinement or by leveraging vision-language models (ViLs), but they often fail to reconcile the inherent discrepancy between task-specific knowledge from black-box models and language-aligned semantic priors of ViLs, resulting in suboptimal integration and degraded adaptation performance. To address this challenge, we propose adaptive Dual-Teacher Distillation with Subnetwork Rectification (DDSR), a framework that explicitly reconciles these complementary yet inconsistent knowledge sources. DDSR employs an adaptive prediction fusion strategy to integrate predictions from the black-box source model and a ViL, generating reliable pseudo-labels for the target domain. A subnetwork-based regularization mechanism mitigates overfitting to noisy supervision by enforcing output consistency and gradient divergency. Furthermore, progressively improved target predictions iteratively refine both pseudo-labels and ViL prompts, enhancing semantic alignment. Finally, class-wise prototypes are used to further optimize target predictions via self-training. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that DDSR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including those with access to source data or source model parameters.
evidence_items.title: Adaptive Dual-Teacher Distillation with Subnetwork Rectification for Bridging Semantic Gaps in Black-Box Domain Adaptation

evidence_items.summary: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) requires a model to continually learn new classes without forgetting old ones. A common and efficient solution freezes a pre-trained model and employs lightweight adapters, whose parameters are often forced to be orthogonal to prevent inter-task interference. However, we argue that this parameter-constraining method is detrimental to plasticity. To this end, we propose Semantic-Guided Dynamic Sparsification (SGDS), a novel method that proactively guides the activation space by governing the orientation and rank of its subspaces through targeted sparsification. Specifically, SGDS promotes knowledge transfer by encouraging similar classes to share a compact activation subspace, while simultaneously preventing interference by assigning non-overlapping activation subspaces to dissimilar classes. By sculpting class-specific sparse subspaces in the activation space, SGDS effectively mitigates interference without imposing rigid constraints on the parameter space. Extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of SGDS.
evidence_items.title: Semantic-Guided Dynamic Sparsification for Pre-Trained Model-based Class-Incremental Learning

evidence_items.summary: Most engineering problems involve complex multi-step derivations through checkable intermediate quantities. Grading only the final answer misjudges LLMs, crediting correct answers reached through flawed steps and penalizing wrong answers built on mostly sound ones. Yet, existing benchmarks such as SuperGPQA and EEE-Bench score only final answers, and step-level ones such as TPS-CalcBench rely on LLM judges or human graders, or cover a single domain. We therefore introduce EngTrace, a symbolic benchmark for verifiable process evaluation of engineering reasoning. Its 150 expert-certified templates, spanning five branches, 15 domains, and 42 areas, generate each problem with a gold reasoning trace, so that every intermediate quantity is known exactly. We design and validate an evaluator that checks final answers, coverage of the gold trace's intermediate quantities (milestones), and displayed arithmetic, mostly without an LLM judge. Across 11 LLMs, final answers barely separate the strongest models, while their derivations differ. Wrong answers still state about half of the gold milestones, and domain experts trace most wrong answers to calculation slips, with conceptual errors rarer on easy problems than on harder ones. Overall, as LLMs near the final-answer ceiling, checking derivations, as EngTrace does, reveals differences that final answers miss.
evidence_items.title: EngTrace: A Symbolic Benchmark for Verifiable Process Evaluation of Engineering Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: We address multi-reference visual place recognition (VPR), where reference sets captured under varying conditions are used to improve localization performance. While deep learning with large-scale training improves robustness, increasing data diversity and model complexity incur extensive computational cost during training and deployment. Descriptor-level fusion via voting or aggregation avoids training, but often targets multi-sensor setups or relies on heuristics with limited gains under appearance and viewpoint change. We propose a training-free, descriptor-agnostic approach that jointly models places using multiple reference descriptors via matrix decomposition into basis representations, enabling projection-based residual matching. We also introduce SotonMV, a benchmark for multi-viewpoint VPR captured over time. Our method improves Recall@1 by up to $\approx$18% over conventional single-reference set matching on appearance-change datasets, and matches or outperforms existing multi-reference baselines across most appearance-change settings. For viewpoint-change datasets, our method supports matching when viewpoint is distributed among the references, with the benefit depending on reference set coverage of the query conditions. On unconstrained reference sets, we additionally observe gains of $\approx$5%, demonstrating strong generalization while remaining computationally lightweight.
evidence_items.title: Joint Multi-Condition Representation Modelling via Matrix Factorisation for Visual Place Recognition

evidence_items.summary: Monitoring cattle behaviour provides valuable insights into animal health, productivity and welfare. However, robust behaviour recognition in real-world farm environments remains challenging because well-annotated livestock video datasets are scarce and agricultural surveillance footage differs substantially from large-scale pretraining data. To address these challenges, we propose Cattle-CLIP, a domain-adaptive vision-language framework based on Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP), which reformulates cattle behaviour recognition as a cross-modal semantic alignment task. Cattle-CLIP incorporates a temporal integration module that extends image-level contrastive pretraining to video-based behaviour understanding and promotes consistent semantic alignment across time. To reduce domain discrepancy, customised data augmentation and behaviour-oriented prompts are employed. We also construct CattleBehaviours6, a curated dataset containing 1,905 annotated clips from six indoor behaviours: feeding, drinking, standing-self-grooming, standing-ruminating, lying-self-grooming and lying-ruminating. The dataset provides standardised ethogram definitions for model training, evaluation and future livestock behaviour research. Cattle-CLIP was evaluated under supervised and few-shot learning settings, with particular emphasis on data-constrained behaviour recognition. In supervised experiments, the model achieved 96.1% accuracy across six behaviours and showed high precision and recall for feeding, drinking and standing-ruminating. It also maintained promising few-shot performance with limited labelled data, demonstrating the potential of multimodal learning for cattle behaviour recognition in data-constrained farm environments.
evidence_items.title: Cattle-CLIP: A Multimodal Framework for Dairy Cattle Behaviour Recognition from Video

evidence_items.summary: Driving behavior varies across individuals, yet most existing driving datasets do not preserve driver identity or control for factors that may affect driving style. We introduce the Personalized Driving Behavior (PDB) dataset, a multimodal dataset collected from 9 drivers using the same vehicle and route under comparable conditions. PDB includes data from a 128-line LiDAR, external and driver-facing cameras, GNSS, IMU, CAN-bus signals, and heart-rate measurements, with 111,060 frames of LiDAR point cloud data and more than 1.33 million images. Based on these recordings, we construct PDB-Traj, a personalized trajectory prediction benchmark with 1,309 10-second trajectory segments sampled at 10 Hz. Each segment includes the ego trajectory, surrounding-agent trajectories, and driver identity. We further introduce Gated Selective Personalization (Gate-SP), a driver-aware baseline that selectively incorporates driver identity into trajectory prediction. Experiments on PDB-Traj provide reference results for personalized motion forecasting and show that driver information can improve prediction when applied selectively. PDB and PDB-Traj provide a benchmark for studying driver-specific behavior and personalized trajectory prediction.
evidence_items.title: PDB: Not All Drivers Are the Same -- A Personalized Dataset for Understanding Driving Behavior

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides 10,000 reproducible instances of the one-dimensional Bin Packing Problem, accompanied by solver-certified integer and linear programming optima, deterministic heuristic packings, optimality certificates, and associated metadata. In the Bin Packing Problem, items with positive integer weights must be assigned to identical bins of a fixed capacity. Every item must be packed exactly once, without exceeding any bin’s capacity. The objective is to minimise the number of bins used. The collection supports computational experiments in combinatorial optimisation, integer programming, linear programming relaxations, approximation algorithms, packing heuristics, and lower-bound techniques. It also provides a resource for algorithm benchmarking and teaching in operations research and computer science. The benchmark includes ten item counts: n = 12, 20, 28, 40, 60, 80, 120, 200, 400, and 800, with bin capacities of 100, 500, or 1,000. Ten instance families are represented: uniform, small-item dominated, large-item dominated, bimodal, clustered, near-half-capacity, near-capacity with fillers, complementary pairs, planted feasible packings, and search-selected quartets. Each family contains 1,000 instances, with 100 at each item count. The search-selected family deliberately targets the recorded heuristics and supports stress testing rather than unbiased estimates of their general performance. Each instance includes its exact ordered item weights and capacity, optimal IP and LP objective values, a verified optimal packing, integrality gaps, generation seed and parameters, structural statistics, solver settings, runtimes, and supporting bounds and certificates. Five deterministic heuristic solutions are supplied: Next Fit, First Fit, Best Fit, First Fit Decreasing, and Best Fit Decreasing. Every instance is feasible and has solver-certified IP and LP optima.
evidence_items.title: Bin Packing Benchmark Dataset

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains supplementary data supporting the study “In vitro evaluation of Chios mastic gum cytotoxicity in canine cancer cell lines.” The Excel workbook contains six supplementary tables reporting the effects of three Chios mastic gum preparations—terpenoid-rich preparation, mastic oil, and powdered mastic gum—on canine cancer cell viability assessed using the MTT assay. The worksheets correspond to the following cell lines:• Table S1: AXA, canine transitional cell carcinoma.• Table S2: AXC, canine transitional cell carcinoma.• Table S3: ORI, canine transitional cell carcinoma.• Table S4: NK, canine transitional cell carcinoma.• Table S5: DENNY, canine hemangiosarcoma.• Table S6: 17CM98, canine malignant melanoma. The workbook includes individual cell viability measurements for untreated controls, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) vehicle controls, and treatment groups, together with absorbance measurements used for concentration–response analyses and estimation of half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC₅₀). Treatment groups include concentrations of 5, 25, 50, 100, and 200 µg/mL. Concentrations are expressed in µg/mL, and normalized cell viability is expressed as a percentage. “Abs570” denotes absorbance at 570 nm. Abbreviations used in the workbook include T (terpenoid preparation), Ol (oil preparation), Pw (powder preparation), DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide), and IC₅₀ (half-maximal inhibitory concentration). The dataset is provided as an Excel workbook (.xlsx) within a ZIP archive. Experimental methods and statistical procedures are described in the accompanying manuscript.

evidence_items.summary: Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce SPARC (Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.
evidence_items.title: SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus

evidence_items.summary: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, making it better aligned with human-AI collaborative creation than single-turn editing. However, constructing high-quality multi-turn training data remains challenging, as conventional sequential rollout accumulates errors and introduces visual-quality drift across editing turns. To address this challenge, we introduce MTEdit, a multi-turn image editing dataset built through a pipeline centered on packed trajectory canvas (PTC) generation. By jointly generating multiple editing states within a unified visual context, this pipeline reduces visual-quality drift across turns. Covering both step-wise and context-aware editing scenarios, MTEdit comprises 500K multi-turn image editing trajectories, with up to 8 turns and an average of 5.38 turns per trajectory, making it one of the most extensive datasets for multi-turn image editing. We further introduce MTEdit-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate both scenarios by assessing models' ability to follow editing instructions, maintain content consistency, resist visual-quality drift, and effectively use historical context across turns. Using MTEdit, we fine-tune Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal to obtain Qwen-Image-MTEdit. On MTEdit-Bench, we evaluate a broad range of closed-source and open-source image editing models, including Qwen-Image-MTEdit. Experimental results show that Qwen-Image-MTEdit achieves the best performance among the evaluated open-source models, demonstrating the effectiveness of MTEdit in improving models' multi-turn image editing capabilities.
evidence_items.title: MTEdit: Packed Trajectories Beat Rollouts for Multi-Turn Image Editing

evidence_items.summary: Making a conference poster is visual coding in miniature: an entire paper must be compressed onto a single page, which exercises summarization, visual design, and code implementation at once, using nothing beyond the paper itself. Yet benchmarks for this task in the context of visual coding remain scarce: existing resources are small and annotated only with layout boxes, so evaluation must fall back on VLM-as-judge or human checklists rather than objective render-and-compare, and the generation methods they support design layouts from scratch, leaving human-crafted posters unusable as either a retrievable design library or as verified supervision. We introduce RAP (Reconstruct A Poster), a dataset and benchmark for paper-to-poster generation as a visual coding task. RAP contains 25K+ verified paper-poster pairs from various machine learning conferences held between 2022 and 2026, annotated with a three-level content taxonomy, plus a held-out benchmark of 150 test papers each paired with its human poster. A fully automated derendering pipeline turns each poster into styled HTML/CSS of typed, refillable slots, so every sample is a paper-poster-markup triplet verifiable by rendering against the source poster. The corpus serves both inference and training: PosterRAG, a training-free multi-agent pipeline, retrieves an exemplar and refills its slots without touching layout or styling, while an SFT+RL recipe trains a dedicated model from the same triplets. An online demo is available at https://reconstruct-a-poster.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: RAP: A Dataset for Paper-to-Poster Generation via Declarative Markup from Human-Crafted Exemplars

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating agents by outcomes alone can obscure the capabilities that produce them. This problem is especially pronounced in evolving environments, where outcomes reflect a closed-loop interaction between agent behavior and changing external conditions. We introduce LiveMACEBench, a process-aware benchmark that uses live financial markets as a naturally evolving testbed for persistent LLM agents. Five frontier LLMs operate along continuous trajectories under matched Tool Use, Persistent Memory, Rule Following, and Multi-Agent Collaboration configurations. We evaluate them through both realized outcomes and mechanism-specific diagnostics derived from complete decision traces. Across 30 days of live evaluation, we find a pronounced outcome-capability gap: realized returns often diverge from capability-specific measurements, and similar outcomes can arise from markedly different patterns of mechanism use. Trace-level diagnostics further expose distinct bottlenecks across capabilities, demonstrating that mechanism access, effective mechanism use, and downstream performance are not interchangeable measures of agent capability. LiveMACEBench makes this distinction measurable, turning live markets from a performance leaderboard into a diagnostic environment for agent capability
evidence_items.title: LiveMACE: Process-Aware Evaluation of LLM Agent Capabilities in Evolving Markets

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVES
To present and describe the design, data collection framework, and interim cohort characteristics of the PENIMA project, a multicentre initiative establishing a clinically annotated penile lesion image repository to support future artificial intelligence (AI)-driven decision-support development - and to encourage urology and dermatology colleagues working with penile lesions to participate in the project.


PATIENTS AND METHODS
Prospective participant inclusion commenced in March 2023 across Scandinavian urological and dermatological departments. Patients with penile anatomy undergoing clinically indicated genital examination are invited to participate and provide oral and written consent as defined by local authority regulations. Clinical photographs and structured metadata are collected. Lesion classification is based on a specialist evaluation, clinical follow-up and histopathology when available. Images are pseudonymised and annotated using a secure, containerised Computer Vision Annotation Tool (CVAT) environment. Supervised machine-learning model development using convolutional neural networks is planned with patient-level dataset partitioning and evaluation using standard diagnostic performance metrics. The study was approved by relevant local authorities, and the approval number is 1-10-72-150-22.


RESULTS
As of February 2026, 1125 participants and approximately 7000 images have been included. In all, 40% represented normal anatomical variants. Among lesional cases, 33% are clinically assessed as benign, 13% premalignant, and 8% malignant; 22% of all cases have histopathological verification. Concordance between clinical suspicion and histopathology is highest for penile carcinoma (84.6%, 95% confidence interval 75.0-91.0%).


CONCLUSION
The PENIMA project includes a multicentre, clinically grounded image repository reflecting real-world penile lesion presentations. The feasible and successful infrastructure provides a foundation for future development and validation of image-based clinical decision-support tools.
evidence_items.title: The PENIMA project: artificial intelligence decision-support tool for penile lesions - protocol paper and invitation to participate.

The road-damage reports are synthetic constructs described in the article, not field observations. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors.
