evidence_items.summary: Hate speech detection in online environments poses significant challenges due to the nuanced and evolving nature of hate speech and the complexities of real-time communication. This study evaluates whether zero-shot large language models (LLMs), including Claude, Gemini 2.0, ChatGPT-o1, and ChatGPT-4o, can support the annotation of gaming-specific hate speech. We compare individual models, a multi-model collective, and TF-IDF–Logistic Regression classifier against an operational human-majority reference on 1,178 Dota 2 chat messages. We also examine whether ChatGPT-generated messages improve the traditional classifier when used exclusively as training-time augmentation, with full-archive augmentation and SMOTE as comparators. Among the automated approaches, the four-model collective achieved the highest accuracy and macro-F1 but did not uniformly outperform the strongest individual LLMs. For the class-sensitive measures, synthetic-data composition mattered more than volume. A post-hoc qualitative analysis identified recurring disagreement patterns and model-specific difficulties. Targeted augmentation achieved higher accuracy than SMOTE. The findings show that class-aware LLM generation can provide a competitive alternative to feature-space oversampling for lightweight classifiers, while zero-shot LLMs are best positioned as complementary annotation tools under human oversight.
evidence_items.title: Improving the Hate Speech Annotation Process with Large Language Models

organizations: School of Automation and Intelligent Sensing, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China
evidence_items.summary: Explicit ratio prompts can request intermediate writing styles, but endpoint classification does not reveal proportional responses at internal ratios. We present a geometric protocol using model-specific endpoints and shared references in external sentence-embedding spaces. It excludes mechanically perfect endpoints from primary errors, retains unclipped projections, and separates axial calibration error from normalized off-axis drift. StyleBlend-Bench contains eight style axes and 320 scenarios. Five Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 checkpoints generated 33,600 texts over seven ratios and three seeds; three encoders produced 100,800 geometric records. An external GPT generator adds 6719 usable texts. A full five-model prompt-by-temperature experiment contains 95,994 usable condition records. Shared-reference BGE-M3 calibration error ranges from 0.176 to 0.212; other encoder/reference choices change model ordering. Two automatic evaluators correlate strongly in style intensity (r = 0.910), but content-pass agreement is 76.2%. The trajectories were rarely one-dimensional: first-component variance ranged from 0.349 to 0.408 and ordered path-length ratios from 4.64 to 5.20. The protocol diagnoses model response under specified anchors and encoders; it does not establish a human perceptual scale or absolute cross-model style coordinate.
evidence_items.title: Geometric Diagnostics for Continuous Style Control in Large Language Models

organizations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, National Clinical Research Center for Oral Diseases, Shanghai Research Institute of Stomatology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for oncology decision support, but open-ended treatment planning poses a measurement problem: a clinically defensible recommendation may differ from a historical plan, and different automated metrics may reward different properties of the same output. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) may improve evidence grounding, but its contribution cannot be inferred without controlled ablation. We evaluated how four archived RAG-enabled LLM configurations agreed with clinician treatment plans for oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and whether apparent model ranking depended on the evaluation method. Methods This single-center retrospective evaluation used the same 100-case OSCC study set for four archived configurations (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Doubao, and Qwen). Generated treatment plans were compared with archived clinician plans using a DeepSeek-based LLM-judge score, m3e-base embedding cosine similarity, ROUGE-1 recall, and an archived blinded five-physician rating protocol. Cohort descriptors were audited from the de-identified case register. Because complete case-level metric arrays and the case-by-rater matrix were not retained, model comparisons were summarized descriptively and no unsupported paired inference was reconstructed. Results The cohort had a mean age of 59.5 years (SD 13.6); 65% of cases were male and 69% were source-coded N0. Model ordering differed by automated metric: Qwen had the highest mean LLM-judge score (0.809; DeepSeek-R1, 0.807), Doubao had the highest mean embedding similarity (0.8489), and Claude had the highest mean ROUGE-1 recall (0.2729). No configuration was uniformly best. The archived clinician-rating summary showed a different descriptive pattern, but formal inter-rater reliability and paired model comparisons could not be recomputed from the available archive.
evidence_items.title: Metric-dependent evaluation of a retrieval-augmented large language model workflow for oral squamous cell carcinoma treatment planning: a retrospective study

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Urology education must prepare learners to integrate anatomical visualization, diagnostic reasoning, technical performance, communication, and ethical judgment, often under restricted working hours and limited access to high-fidelity cases. This viewpoint argues that large language models (LLMs) and metaverse-related technologies should be integrated as complementary, supervised educational tools rather than treated as autonomous replacements for educators or clinical experience. LLMs can support cognitive apprenticeship, documentation practice, assessment, and communication simulations, whereas extended reality, cloud computing, and virtual digital humans can support spatial, procedural, and remote learning. Our aim is to articulate 3 key messages: first, the educational value of these technologies depends on alignment with defined urological competencies; second, implementation should proceed in stages from governed data infrastructure to intelligent interaction and immersive multimodal training; and third, educational effectiveness must be established through prospective evaluations of transfer to clinical performance, not through technical novelty alone. We emphasize the need for rigorous randomized controlled trials, identify requirements for haptic and biomechanical fidelity, and discuss hallucination, bias, privacy, accountability, and deskilling. The responsible future of intelligent urology education will therefore require collaboration among learners, educators, clinicians, engineers, ethicists, institutions, and professional bodies.
evidence_items.title: Integrating Large Language Models and Metaverse-Related Technologies in Urology Education: Viewpoint

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for clinical tasks, but safe use requires reliable uncertainty estimates as well as high accuracy. We tested eight general-purpose LLMs on 100 validated neurology board-style multiple-choice questions and compared three confidence signals: self-reported confidence, critique-implied confidence from an independent model instance, and consistency-based confidence from repeated sampling. Accuracy varied from 45% (Llama 3.1 8B) to 92% (Gemini 3 Flash/Pro), but confidence was generally overestimated, particularly in lower-accuracy models. Consistency-based confidence provided the best discrimination between correct and incorrect answers (pooled AUROC 0.74), outperforming self-report, although calibration differences between methods were not significant. Calibration should therefore be reported alongside accuracy when clinical LLMs are evaluated.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy and confidence calibration of large language models on neurology board-style questions

evidence_items.summary: Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) requires sustained patient education, self-management, medication use, pulmonary rehabilitation, symptom monitoring, and guideline-concordant clinical management. Large language models (LLMs) may expand access to conversational health information, but their value depends on more than factual accuracy. Objective: To map empirical evidence on LLMs and LLM-based generative artificial intelligence systems in COPD-related care and health management, summarize application domains and evaluation outcomes, and identify priorities for future research. Methods: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported using PRISMA-ScR. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, CINAHL, and PsycINFO were searched from inception through September 10, 2026. Empirical studies evaluating an LLM or LLM-based generative AI system in COPD-related patient education, health information, pulmonary rehabilitation, medication management, or guideline-based clinical management were eligible. Data were charted and synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results: The search identified 327 records; 34 duplicates were removed, and 293 records underwent title/abstract screening. Of these, 281 were excluded, and 12 full-text reports were assessed. Four full-text reports were excluded, leaving eight studies. Five studies focused primarily on patient education or health information, one on pulmonary rehabilitation, one on COPD medication management, and one on guideline-based clinical management. Accuracy and information quality were the most common outcomes. LLMs often produced clinically acceptable responses, but limitations included incomplete information, high reading grade levels, outdated guideline references, response variability, and differences across models and task formats.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Care and Health Management: A Scoping Review

evidence_items.summary: Against the backdrop of global climate change and the green development transition, the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has brought new opportunities for the green and low-carbon transformation of the economy and society. Taking the construction of the National New Generation Artificial Intelligence Innovation Development Pilot Zones launched in 2019 as a quasi-natural experiment, this paper systematically evaluates the impact effects and mechanisms of AI development on urban green economic development using a difference-in-differences (DID) model, based on panel data of 35 Chinese cities from 2011 to 2024. The findings are as follows: First, the AI pilot policy significantly improves the level of urban green economic development, with a policy effect of 0.0523, significant at the 1% level; this conclusion remains valid after a series of tests including endogeneity treatment, robustness checks, placebo tests, and PSM-DID. Second, the parallel trends test shows that before the policy implementation, the green economic development trends of the treatment and control groups remained parallel; after the policy implementation, the policy effect emerged immediately and strengthened year by year, rising from 0.0321 to 0.0756, exhibiting notable persistence and cumulative effects. Third, the mechanism analysis shows that AI development promotes green economic development mainly through three channels: industrial structure upgrading, digital inclusive finance development, and human capital enhancement, with mediating effects of 0.0345, 0.0289, and 0.0123, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Research on the Impact of Artificial Intelligence Development on Green Economic Development——Empirical Evidence from the National New Generation Artificial Intelligence Innovation Development Pilot Zones

evidence_items.summary: Assessment is most powerful when understood as a leadership-driven process of continuous improvement—iterative, evidence-informed, and oriented toward genuine learning rather than compliance. However, the coordination costs of meaningful assessment have historically exceeded most programs’ capacity to sustain it. This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, and in particular retrieval-augmented reasoning environments, can function as leadership-support tools that change the conditions under which assessment becomes practically feasible without displacing the human judgment it requires. Drawing on leadership education and assessment scholarship, we develop a three-level framework—individual and course, program, and institutional—and present six practice-based use cases illustrating AI-supported assessment at each level, including an AI-populated curriculum alignment matrix and an AI-assisted synthesis of external program reviews. We also directly address the tensions practitioners must navigate: data contamination from AI-generated student work, reliability-validity trade-offs, the limitations of AI detection tools, and the faculty professional development gap. Implications for assessment leaders are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Leading Continuous Improvement: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Assessment in Higher Education

evidence_items.summary: Geological sequestration of carbon dioxide is an important strategy for reducing anthropogenic carbon emissions and mitigating global warming. Basalt reservoirs offer a promising route for long-term CO<sub>2</sub> sequestration because injected CO<sub>2</sub> can be converted into stable carbonate minerals through in-situ water-rock reactions. This paper focuses on four main aspects: the basic mineralization principles of CO<sub>2</sub> sequestration in basalt, the major methods for evaluating basalt geological sequestration potential, the coupled evolution of reservoir porosity and permeability during dissolution and precipitation, and the assessment results for basalt CO<sub>2</sub> geological sequestration potential in China. Particular attention is given to the growing use of computer-based geochemical, reactive-transport, physical, and Monte Carlo simulations to connect water-rock reaction mechanisms with time-dependent mineral trapping and engineering-scale capacity estimates, as well as to emerging artificial-intelligence and remote-sensing approaches for regional basalt mapping. By comparing theoretical models, experimental constraints, numerical simulations, and regional evaluation data, the review shows that basalt sequestration capacity is controlled jointly by mineral reactivity, connected pore space, fluid migration, permeability evolution, and engineering-scale effective coefficients. Computer simulation can reduce the gap between theoretical and effective capacity, while AI-assisted remote sensing can improve preliminary identification of prospective basalt areas; both should be integrated with field and laboratory validation.
evidence_items.title: Applications of computer simulation and artificial intelligence in CO₂ geological sequestration

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) recently appeared as an issue of its time which has been changing the educational landscape at a considerable rate and opening new pathways and challenges for educators and learners. Therefore, in terms of GenAI for education this bibliometric analysis will characterize the change and development by mapping trends and patterns, examining prevalent subject areas in academia interest. Following the established criteria, we ran a systematic search on Scopus database with the identification and analysis of 121 peer-reviewed documents (journal articles, review articles and conference papers; selection reported with reference to the PRISMA 2020 guideline) published between January 2023 and March 2025 related to GenAI applied in education. The thematic labels attached to the algorithmically generated VOSviewer clusters were assigned by the researchers, and interpretations of regional patterns are presented as tentative. The article features papers discussing ways to use GenAI in learner-centered teaching, curriculum development and assessment. The findings reveal a rapid increase in research output between 2023 (23 articles) and 2024 (67 articles), followed by 31 articles in the first quarter of 2025, and substantial international collaboration (34% of the articles). Moreover, the thematic analysis shows that pedagogical integration and instructional design (55.4% of the articles), assessment and academic integrity (44.6%) and ethical and societal implications (39.7%) are the most prominent themes, with a shift from ethical and assessment concerns in 2023 towards pedagogical integration and learning outcomes in 2024-2025. Research affiliated with the United States, the United Kingdom, China and Germany dominates the corpus, whereas research from Latin America and Africa appears under-represented.
evidence_items.title: Generative artificial intelligence in education mapping research trends and future directions

evidence_items.summary: Avaliar modelos de linguagem em domínios específicos, como o Direito do Consumidor, é um desafio devido à escassez de recursos padronizados em português brasileiro. Para resolver esse problema, introduzimos o OABench-Consumidor, um benchmark composto exclusivamente por questões de Direito do Consumidor da primeira fase do Exame de Ordem Unificado (OAB), cobrindo as edições de 2010.1 a 2025.2. Este artigo descreve a coleta e a estruturação dos dados. Além disso, a utilidade do benchmark é demonstrada através da avaliação do modelo fundacional Qwen3-8B e de uma versão ajustada. O modelo especializado obteve 64,84% de acurácia (59/91), superando os 51,65% (47/91) do modelo base. O benchmark oferece um recurso direto para avaliar sistemas de Inteligência Artificial nessa subárea do Direito.
evidence_items.title: OABench-Consumidor: Um benchmark para avaliação de modelos de linguagem em Direito do Consumidor

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Contamination by microplastics is an emerging environmental problem that is widely distributed across continental aquatic environments and may cause ecological impacts. This study evaluated the occurrence, concentration, and chemical and morphological characteristics of microplastics in surface waters and sediments from Lake Canaçari, comparing two areas with different land-use patterns within a floodplain system in the Central Amazon. Microplastics were detected in all sampled areas. In surface water, concentrations ranged from 0 (no microplastic particles detected in one sample) to 1,000 microplastics·m⁻ 3 (405 ± 298 microplastics·m⁻ 3 ), while in sediments, they ranged from 7 to 307 microplastics·kg⁻ 1 (77 ± 104 microplastics·kg⁻ 1 ). No significant differences in microplastic concentrations were observed between fishing and human-settlement areas. The particles were predominantly blue fibers (< 1,000 μm). Among the spectroscopically analyzed particles, polyethylene was the most frequently identified polymer, while copper phthalocyanine pigments, including Pigment Blue 15 and Pigment Green 7, were also detected by FTIR and/or Raman spectroscopy. Overall, the results suggest that Lake Canaçari may act as a transport pathway, redistribution zone, and retention compartment for microplastics; however, seasonal sampling is needed to confirm how these processes vary throughout the hydrological cycle. These results reinforce the role of Amazonian floodplain systems in the regional dynamics of microplastics and highlight the need for monitoring and management strategies that incorporate seasonal hydrological connectivity at the basin scale.
evidence_items.title: Microplastic contamination in surface water and sediments of Lake Canaçari, Central Amazon, during the dry season

evidence_items.summary: Hallucination-detection systems are usually judged by a single headline metric, computed under a benchmark design that determines what that metric can show. This paper’s contribution is not a detection algorithm — structural coherence scoring is established — but a methodology for measuring exactly what a benchmark proves and what it does not, applied to the SAS Multimetric Tribunal: a seven-module, GPU-free structural classifier combining lexical, entity-mutation, curvature, and logical-inversion signals via a cascading multiplicative penalty (\(\kappa {D} = 0.56\), \(\kappa {R} = 0.15\)). On a stratified 1,800-pair benchmark (HaluEval-Dialogue, HaluEval-QA, TruthfulQA), the tribunal reaches F1 = 98.99% with zero false positives under an A\(\rightarrow\)A identical-text sanity check. We report this figure and then show, using a format-controlled negative (N1) on the same 1,800 IDs, that it measures format asymmetry between source and response rather than hallucination detection. The tribunal flags 1,569 of 1,800 verbatim correct answers presented alone (87.2%), and in HaluEval-QA scores the correct answer as more anomalous than the hallucinated response. Three further findings follow from the same audit. (i) A per-module analysis shows the tribunal’s seven-module core has no content-sensitive module (prior to the optional R3.1 guard): the one module designed to capture semantic divergence (cre isi) gives the same per-ID score whether the response is byte-identical or completely different. (ii) The 87.97-point advantage of multiplicative combination over weighted averaging reported in v4 is an artifact of threshold calibration; under per-scheme thresholds on format-matched negatives, both schemes converge to F1 \(\approx 0.69\) and the multiplicative scheme is worse by AUROC.
evidence_items.title: SAS Multimetric Tribunal: What a Hallucination Benchmark Measures and What It Does Not — A Format-Controlled Audit of Structural Classification

organizations: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Near-infrared (NIR) optical imaging can interrogate centimeter-scale tissue through absorption and multiple scattering, but quantitative interpretation depends critically on the fidelity of the forward photon-transport model. We present an output-verified Monte Carlo eXtreme (MCX) workflow for a homogeneous 60 × 60 × 60 mm³ breast-tissue phantom and explicitly separate nominal configuration, executed simulation state, and post-processed observables. The analyzed execution launched 1,000,000 photon histories and recorded 704 detector events, corresponding to a detection efficiency of 0.0704% (binomial 95% CI, 0.0652–0.0756%). The executed optical parameters were µa = 0.0005 mm⁻¹, µs = 1.0 mm⁻¹, g = 0.9, and n = 1.4. Detected-photon path lengths were strongly right-skewed, with a mean of 53.17 mm, a median of 31.46 mm, and a maximum of 732.07 mm. A critical correction to the earlier analysis is that the reported 60-point fluence profile is treated here as a cross-axis profile rather than a depth profile: the source is specified at (30,30,0) mm and MCX uses explicit x–y–z coordinate conventions, so interpreting the profile as z-depth was not justified by the supplied execution record. The manuscript therefore reports the profile as an output-coordinate diagnostic. An independent analytical diffusion-shape check, performed outside the near-source region, gives Pearson r = 0.986 for the normalized profiles, supporting qualitative transport consistency without claiming absolute fluence validation. The study is intentionally a computational benchmark rather than a tumor-detection study. Its principal contribution is a reproducibility framework that makes the executed optical properties, coordinate interpretation, normalization, detector statistics, and derived photon-path observables auditable.
evidence_items.title: Output-Verified GPU Monte Carlo Modeling of Near-Infrared Photon Transport in a Homogeneous Breast-Tissue Phantom: A Reproducible Computational Benchmark

organizations: The Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine;
evidence_items.summary: We present an interactive Data Integrator to facilitate uniform data processing and integration with datasets generated by the NIH funded MorPhiC (Molecular Phenotypes of Null Alleles in Cells) program. In the dataset identification step, users can select published bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets generated by the MorPhiC program, specify external datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository, or upload raw RNA-seq data. Subsequently, users can select a subset of samples and indicate experimental design by assigning groups to samples. External data will then be processed using the MorPhiC approved bulk RNA-seq analytical pipeline, and differential expression will be inferred. Users also have the option to download the uniformly processed counts table.
evidence_items.title: Interactive Data Integrator for Uniform Data Processing in the MorPhiC Program

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is moving hospital quality reporting to FHIR-based digital measures, with evidence so far mostly from synthetic test cases. This study asked whether two hospital-harm measures, severe hypoglycemia (CMS816) and severe hyperglycemia (CMS871), run over a complete hospital database without changing their results, and which data problems change them. Materials and Methods Under a preregistered plan, CMS’s draft FHIR specifications were run with fqm-execution on MIMIC-IV-on-FHIR (431,231 stays, 2008–2019). A pipeline that cuts each patient’s record into per-stay slices was compared stay by stay with the unmodified engine. In 88,234 stays from 2017–2019, measure-derived checks were applied and both measures rerun under alternative mappings and scenarios. Results The pipeline matched the unmodified engine on all 1,994 stays compared (discordance upper bound 0.19%); whole-record evaluation needed at least 98 times more CMS816 engine time. All 431,231 stays ran in 5.6 hours for US$4.52. Medication-mapping choices moved up to 4.3% of CMS816’s denominator while its rate changed under 0.1 points. In exploratory analyses, bedside glucose results without a unit hid 57 of 130 severe hypoglycemic stays (CMS816 0.70% vs 1.24% with mg/dL assigned; difference 0.54 points, 95% CI 0.41–0.68), and counting observation stays as inpatient doubled CMS816’s denominator and events alike. Discussion With identical execution, every change came from the data. Checks built from the measure logic found these problems; profile validation did not. Conclusion What these measures report depends on data readiness, which should be tested before FHIR reporting becomes mandatory.
evidence_items.title: Identical results, hidden data problems: running CMS's digital quality measures on real hospital data

evidence_items.summary: Deep learning has driven rapid progress in medical image analysis, with methods for tasks such as organ segmentation, anomaly detection, and radiology report generation now matching or surpassing expert performance on several benchmarks. While many methods are released as open source, their routine adoption by clinicians and medical researchers remains limited. The bottleneck is not a lack of capable tools, but the absence of infrastructure to make them accessible to non-technical users. To break this barrier, we present MedMCP, an agentic framework that solves this last-mile problem along two axes: (1) a local agentic workspace that lets users apply state-of-the-art image analysis methods through natural language, and (2) a community-driven tool ecosystem that lets developers deploy and distribute capabilities as validated, independently testable servers. MedMCP enforces a strict orchestration-execution boundary in which a local language model translates user intent into workflow plans, while all image analysis is delegated to domain-specific tools. The framework runs entirely on-premise, every side-effecting operation passes through a human-in-the-loop permission gate, and a full provenance trail links each output to the tools, parameters, and inputs that produced it. An inspectable workspace lets users verify intermediate results rather than blindly trusting the agent, and completed sessions distill into deterministic, shareable workflows that re-execute without the agent, turning one-off interactions into reproducible analyses. This paper introduces the project's general idea and describes the design principles that guide its development. Beyond a single toolkit, we envision MedMCP as a community-driven platform where each contributed tool becomes easily accessible, compounding individual efforts into shared capability.
evidence_items.title: MedMCP: An Open Agentic Ecosystem for Medical Imaging Workflows

organizations: Assistant Professor& HoD, Department of Information Technology, Rajiv Gandhi College of Engineering and Technology, Puducherry, India
UG Scholar, Department of Information Technology, Rajiv Gandhi College of Engineering and Technology, Puducherry, India.
evidence_items.summary: Diagnosing production incidents is still largely manual: on-call engineers gather logs, errors and deployment history from separate tools before they can reason about a cause. Large language models (LLMs) can suggest root causes, but a model that sees only an incident summary lacks evidence, and an unchecked suggestion can mislead. This paper aims to give an LLM agent the evidence it needs while keeping a human in control. We present Phase 1 of an open, four-module platform: a non-blocking Java SDK that captures exceptions, latency and deployments; a multi-tenant Spring Boot backend that groups repeated errors into incidents by stack hash; a FastAPI service in which a tool-calling LLM investigates each incident only through audited APIs; and a dashboard where an operator approves or rejects every suggestion. We evaluate it by injecting seven kinds of real faults into an instrumented service. All 21 trials were detected, with mean detection times of 8–12 s for exception faults and 25–45 s for resource faults, and no incident was raised in 8 min of fault-free operation. The SDK added a median of 14 µs per captured error and stayed non-blocking when the backend was down. A successful investigation used about 11k–24k tokens and two to three minutes; of five graded suggestions, two were correct, two partly correct and one wrong despite a confidence of 0.78. The results show that telemetry-grounded investigation is practical for small teams, and that self-reported confidence must not replace human review.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Incident Response Platform for Cloud Applications: Telemetry-Grounded Root-Cause Investigation with Human Approval

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate left ventricular (LV) segmentation and ejection fraction (EF) estimation from echocardiographic videos are important for cardiovascular risk stratification, but automated methods remain sensitive to domain shift and limited site-specific annotations. We present EchoMed Agent, an imaging-driven framework that integrates MedSAM2, a video segmentation foundation model adapted using rank-4 low-rank adaptation in the mask-decoder attention layers, with a constrained GPT-5.2–based natural-language tool-routing interface for prompt-guided LV segmentation and automated functional assessment. A lightweight axis-regression module, AxisHead, applies mask-guided pooling to frozen vision-transformer features to predict the LV long axis for single-plane area-length volume and EF estimation. The framework was initially trained on EchoNet-Dynamic and subsequently evaluated using few-shot adaptation on an independent Mayo Clinic cohort of 98 studies. With 20 labeled site-specific studies, EchoMed Agent achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.940 and a median absolute EF error of 4.33 percentage points on the Mayo cohort. This Dice score exceeded the 0.932 obtained by an EchoNet-Dynamic–trained MedSAM2 model transferred to Mayo without site-specific adaptation. Overall, 83.3% of evaluated cases had an absolute EF error of no more than 10 percentage points. These findings suggest that parameter-efficient site-specific adaptation can reduce the number of required annotations while maintaining clinically relevant segmentation and EF-estimation accuracy on an independent institutional cohort.
evidence_items.title: EchoMed Agent: A Foundation Model–Based Agentic Framework for Echocardiographic Left Ventricular Segmentation and Functional Assessment
Programme Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Predicting ship turnaround time at ports is an operationally valuable regression problem on heterogeneous, text-rich tabular data. We ask whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can match purpose-built Machine Learning (ML) on this task, using a leakage-controlled pipeline over seven years of Brazilian (ANTAQ) data. On a fixed 200-berthing test set, with 20 seeds and seed-paired statistics (Wilcoxon, Cohen’s d), we compare five families that read the same cases: classical ML on engineered tabular features plus multilingual sentence embeddings; frontier LLMs (Qwen3-32B, DeepSeek-V3) prompted zero-, 5and 20-shot; a small generative LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B) fine-tuned on 100–6000 serialized records; an encoder with a regression head fine-tuned on 100–12000 records; and a tabular foundation model (TabFM) reading the raw table in-context. Tuned XGBoost attains R2 ≈ 0.73. Every prompted configuration stays at R2 ≤ 0 and in-context examples do not help; generative fine-tuning barely clears zero, reaching only R2 ≈ 0.10 at 6000 examples. The encoder is the only text regime to rise substantially above R2 = 0, reaching ≈ 0.43 at 12000 examples yet still trailing all ML. In contrast, TabFM, with no task training, matches or beats a data-matched XGBoost at every budget (100–6000; R2 up to ≈ 0.60), leading the low-data regime, though full-data XGBoost still wins and TabFM is far costlier at inference. The predictive signal is tabular, not textual: text-only LLMs miss it, whereas a tabular foundation model recovers it in-context and engineered boosting wins at scale.
evidence_items.title: Traditional Machine Learning versus Large Language Models for Predicting Ship Turnaround Times at Brazilian Ports

evidence_items.summary: The rapid growth of short-video platforms has created large collections of visual content that are difficult to organize manually. Video clustering offers a practical way to explore these collections, but its quality depends on representations that capture the meaning of each video, not only its visual appearance. Compact vision-language models can generate useful descriptions, although these descriptions are often too generic to support fine-grained semantic grouping. We introduce a method for improving unsupervised video clustering by building richer semantic representations from short visual descriptions before embedding generation. Instead of relying directly on the initial captions produced by a compact vision-language model, the method expands each description with information about actions, objects, context, intent, scene type, and possible high-level categories. Multiple Large Language Models are used to generate complementary semantic views of the same video, which are then converted into embeddings and clustered without using labels. Experiments on the MSR-VTT benchmark show that enriched descriptions produce more coherent clusters than the original descriptions: the best overall configuration (Claude-enriched descriptions with OpenAI embeddings) reaches an NMI of 0.3740, a 5.71% relative gain over its caption-only baseline, while the largest relative improvement (13.18%) is obtained with Qwen embeddings. The results indicate that LLM-based enrichment helps reduce the semantic gap between visual content and high-level meaning, offering a practical path to organize unlabeled video collections under a known taxonomy.
evidence_items.title: LLM-based Description Enrichment for Short Video Clustering
Evaluating COPD care assistance: a comparative study of ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4.0, and ERNIE bot performance.

evidence_items.summary: Browser agents based on large language models can automate web tasks, but deployment remains constrained by repeated model calls, monetary cost, and privacy risks. In practical settings, agents often process page states that may expose credentials, personal data, internal records, business documents, or authenticated session information. Sending these states and interaction histories to external model APIs can increase the risk of data leakage, unauthorized retention, or unintended disclosure. This paper investigates whether reasoning traces from a stronger teacher model can improve open-weight browser agents without fine-tuning. We propose In-Context Learning Guidance (ICLG), a training-free teacher–student protocol in which the teacher solves representative browser tasks offline and its reasoning traces are converted into reusable prompt-level guidance for similar tasks. The student then uses this guidance during execution while reading the concrete target values from the current browser instance. We evaluate ICLG on MiniWoB++, using GPT-5.1 as the teacher and ten open-weight student variants. ICLG increases solved student-task pairs from 208 to 271 and improves 7 out of 10 students. Ablation results suggest that these gains are not due only to retrying or generic prompt refinement. Overall, the results show that reusable teacher guidance can improve lower-cost browser agents and reduce dependence on proprietary teacher APIs during deployment.
evidence_items.title: In-Context Teacher–Student Guidance for Open-Weight Browser Agents

evidence_items.summary: A segmentação de texto vem sendo amplamente difundida e utilizada para extrair informação relevante de documentos. Essas informações estão distribuídas em diversos tipos de estruturas, que incluem dados heterogêneos. A extração desses dados tem sido ultimamente, utilizada por LLMs (Large Language Models). Porém, os treinamentos dos modelos de linguagem não detém características peculiares de dados mistos, tais como dados lexicais e dados fonéticos. Assim, torna-se um desafio analisar a corretude das transcrições de maneira automatizada por LLMs. Neste estudo, a segmentação textual e extração de informação foi paralelizada em duas principais abordagens com o intuito de avaliar a comparação de uma abordagem simbólica e uma abordagem neural. Os resultados demonstram as vantagens e desvantagens em ambas as abordagens para os tipos de dados mistos.
evidence_items.title: Text segmentation with mixed data: evaluating symbolic and neural approaches

evidence_items.summary: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in finance has enabled automated generation of in-domain texts such as earnings summaries, market analyses, and commentary on regulated disclosures. Generating accurate and accessible financial commentary from material facts poses challenges related to domain-specific language, strict factual faithfulness, and readability. Evaluating such outputs is difficult: traditional automatic metrics overlook financial correctness and adequacy, while human expert assessment is reliable but costly and subjective. This paper proposes a multidimensional evaluation protocol for generating financial commentary in Portuguese and investigates the use of LLMs as evaluators (“LLMs-as-judges”) in this high-stakes, low-resource setting. We systematically compare human expert judgments and LLM-based evaluation preferences, while also investigating complementary dimensions such as writing quality, factuality, usefulness, and simplicity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first proposal of an evaluation protocol for this task in Portuguese. Furthermore, we analyze where LLM judgments align with or diverge from human assessments, providing practical insights and recommendations for evaluation methodologies in financial AI applications.
evidence_items.title: Do LLM Judges Agree with Humans? Evaluating Financial Commentaries from Material Facts
CompKG-FactEval: a knowledge graph comparison-based framework for summarization factual consistency evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Several studies have investigated Large Language Models’ (LLMs) ability to answer questions from national educational assessments. However, specialized domains such as databases remain underexplored. Furthermore, current literature lacks a comprehensive analysis of how multimodal capabilities affect accuracy and stability across multiple runs. This study aims to fill these gaps by evaluating the accuracy and stability of five modern LLMs in solving 25 database questions from POSCOMP, using API requests, with hyperparameter control and five independent runs per configuration. The models investigated were GPT-5 Nano, GPT-5.4, Grok 4.1 Fast, Gemini 3 Flash Preview, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, considering both LaTeX and image inputs. Additionally, we applied non-parametric statistical tests to evaluate the significance of performance differences between these input modalities. The results show that Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview demonstrated the best overall performance, outperforming the other models in both accuracy and consistency across runs, while GPT-5 Nano and Grok 4.1 Fast exhibited significant performance degradation under image inputs. Finally, the findings reinforce the importance of API-based evaluations with multiple independent runs to analyze not only the accuracy but also the reliability of responses generated by LLMs in technical domains.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of LLMs in Answering Questions: A Case Study on POSCOMP

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) in Question-Answering (QA) tasks. However, traditional text-based retrieval may prove insufficient in specialized domains, such as geoscience, where critical information is highly interconnected and distributed across complex concepts, relations, and interpretative descriptions. While Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) addresses part of this limitation by structuring evidence into entity-relation graphs, it remains susceptible to terminological inconsistencies, synonyms, and domain-specific variants. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a controlled empirical study evaluating ontology-enriched GraphRAG for Portuguese geoscience QA. We systematically compared four generation strategies: LLM-only, textual RAG, standard GraphRAG, and ontology-enriched GraphRAG. The ontology-driven approach grounds text-extracted entities in formal reference ontologies using a cascading matching strategy that starts with embedding-based semantic similarity, followed by URI-based, label-based, and alternative-label-based matching. Evaluated across semantic, lexical, contextual, and graph-level metrics, our results confirm that external retrieval is indispensable, as retrieval-based strategies outperform the LLM-only baseline. Textual RAG achieved the strongest lexical overlap, while ontology-enriched GraphRAG achieved the highest Correctness, Completeness, and Contextual Recall. GraphRAG provided stronger grounding and question alignment, as reflected by higher Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy. Beyond these answerand context-level gains, the most substantial effect of ontology enrichment was structural, driving a substantial expansion in graph semantic coverage, graph size, and matching rate. These findings suggest that ontology grounding acts primarily as a powerful enabling mechanism for semantic representation; however, its impact on answer quality depends on retrieval, subgraph selection, and prompt construction.
evidence_items.title: Ontology-Enriched GraphRAG: A Case Study in Portuguese Geoscience Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid advancement of self-supervised learning in computer vision, pretrained models have shown remarkable transferability across a wide range of downstream tasks by effectively leveraging large-scale unlabeled data. However, prevailing approaches predominantly adopt supervised fine-tuning strategies on individual models, often overlooking the potential complementarity between different pretrained models during adaptation. This limitation constrains the further improvement of model performance. To address this, the authors propose a bidirectional mutual learning framework that enables two distinct self-supervised models to be jointly fine-tuned on a target task. By exchanging predictions during training, the models share knowledge and collaboratively enhance their representations. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that their method consistently outperforms conventional full-parameter fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) in classification performance. Notably, the superior results achieved on the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) data set highlight the potential of their method in medical imaging analysis.
evidence_items.title: Mutual learning of self-supervised ViTs for image classification with limited labeled data

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in nuclear medicine are reshaping the evaluation of cardiac amyloidosis, as highlighted by the recent collection published in EJNMMI (collection link: https://link.springer.com/collections/igfdhcddjg). This commentary summarizes key insights from these studies, emphasizing the evolving shift from conventional diagnostic imaging toward a more integrated and comprehensive approach. Emerging developments include novel amyloid PET tracers, improved diagnostic accuracy with SPECT/CT, multimodality imaging strategies, and enhanced assessment of systemic disease burden extending beyond the left ventricle. There is also growing interest in longitudinal monitoring, pre-symptomatic detection, and the role of artificial intelligence. Together, these advances position nuclear medicine as an essential tool for disease characterization, risk stratification, and treatment assessment.
evidence_items.title: Expanding role of nuclear medicine in cardiac amyloidosis: insights from the EJNMMI collection

evidence_items.summary:
This article examines learners’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) with both languagerelated and subject-specific learning processes in the foreign language classroom. The development of critical digital literacy (#CDL), understood as the ability to critically assess and evaluate digital, including AI-generated content, is focused on in the reported research data, a video-taped double 
lesson of an upper-secondary advanced English course. In the lesson, learners used generative AI ChatGPT and DALL-E 3) to design their own campaigns for the promotion of gender equality, and discussed and reflected the appropriateness of AI-generated visual representations. The data analysis draws on video and screen recordings, group discussions, the plenary presentation and the subsequently initiated reflection. Focusing on a critical incident, the analysis shows how learners negotiate meaning by aligning with or distancing themselves from AI-generated artefacts, concomitantly developing, testing, evaluating and reflecting upon prompting strategies. In particular, the data reveal the learners’ critical engagement with AI-generated representations of gender in relation to diversity, equality, justice and intersectional equity as well as implicit and contested beauty ideals. Processes of interpretation, appropriation, emotional engagement and the act of developing and defending a position become visible as learners distance themselves from DALL-E 3’s stereotypical visual worlds and the underlying algorithmic biases of ChatGPT.
evidence_items.title: Die Förderung von Critical Digital Literacy im Englischunterricht am Beispiel visueller Repräsentationen von Gender durch künstliche Intelligenz
Evaluation of chemically activated hydrochar from filter coffee waste for ibuprofen removal: process optimisation using response surface methodology.

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Despite reductions in hospital-associated Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) incidence in Canada and the United States, the incidence of community-associated CDI (CA-CDI) has remained high. We sought to investigate whether neighbourhood-level variation in antibiotic utilization is associated with CA-CDI.


METHOD
We conducted a neighbourhood-level ecological study across 1,520 neighbourhoods in Ontario, Canada. Residents aged ≥66 without hospitalization in the prior 30 days were eligible for inclusion from 2017 to 2023. Antibiotic utilization, CDI cases, and population were identified for each neighbourhood using comprehensive province-wide databases. CA-CDI rate was the outcome (incident cases of CA-CDI/10,000 person-years). Rate of antibiotic utilization (DOT per 1000 person-days) was the primary exposure. The rate-ratio (RR) of CA-CDI associated with increased antibiotic utilization was estimated using negative-binomial regression, adjusting for 8 demographic and health care covariates. We also evaluated risk based on low-, moderate-, and high-risk antibiotic strata based on published literature.


RESULT
We identified 19,757 CA-CDI cases. We observed substantial variation in antibiotic utilization across neighbourhoods (Median=21.1 DOT/1000 person-days; interquartile range [IQR], 16.7-25.6). After adjustments, we observed an association between overall antibiotic utilization (RR=1.13 per 10-point increase in DOT; 95% confidence interval [95%CI], 1.09-1.18). A gradient wherein higher risk antibiotic agents were more strongly associated with CA-CDI was apparent (Low-risk: RR=1.08; 95%CI, 1.01-1.15; Moderate-risk: RR=1.27; 95%CI, 1.15-1.39; High-risk: RR=1.73; 95%CI, 1.13-2.66).


DISCUSSION
Neighbourhoods with higher antibiotic utilization, especially for moderate and high-risk antibiotics, have higher CA-CDI incidence. Reducing variability in neighbourhood antibiotic utilization could help reduce the burden of CDI.
evidence_items.title: Association Between Neighbourhood-level Antibiotic Utilization and the Rate of Community-Associated C. difficile (CA-CDI) Infection: An Ecological Study.

evidence_items.summary: Identification of metabolic markers of prohibited and emerging performance-enhancing substances remains a key challenge in anti-doping analysis, where limitations of conventional in vitro models in resembling authentic physiological conditions exist. Organ-on-a-chip (OoC) systems combining 3D human liver-cell cultures with microfluidic perfusion offer a predictive alternative for human-like drug metabolism. In this study, a HepaRG™-based liver OoC model incorporating hepatic stellate cells was characterized over a three-week period with a focus on cytochrome P450 (CYP)-mediated metabolism. CYP activity, gene expression, and inducibility were assessed for major hepatic CYP isoforms, complemented by pharmacogenomic profiling. Metabolic performance was further evaluated using S107, a non-approved and prohibited doping agent, with metabolite formation being determined by liquid chromatography and high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS/MS) in comparison with published in vitro data. The OoC system maintained stable viability and hepatic functionality throughout the culture period, demonstrating phase-I metabolic competence. Isoform-specific differences in mRNA expression and enzymatic activity highlighted complex regulatory effects within the microphysiological environment, while rifampicin responses confirmed preserved nuclear receptor-mediated inducibility across the system. Functional limitations were observed for CYP2D6 and CYP2B6, which showed absent or restricted activity despite detectable transcriptional signals. For S107, the model generated both phase-I and phase-II metabolites, consistent with literature data from microsomal incubation experiments. Metabolite formation was stable over the three-week period under dynamic perfusion conditions, demonstrating sustained biotransformation capacity. Overall, the HepaRG™ OoC system represents a physiologically relevant in vitro platform for long-term metabolism and demonstrates potential as a predictive tool for anti-doping applications and for elucidating metabolic pathways of emerging performance-enhancing substances.
evidence_items.title: Microphysiological organ-on-a-chip system for anti-doping research: long-term CYP activity characterization and S107 metabolism in a HepaRG™-based 3D liver model.

evidence_items.summary: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.
evidence_items.title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena

evidence_items.summary: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. We use our 3D foundation model, anatomix, to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes and further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific, component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system placed first on the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at https://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.
evidence_items.title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration

evidence_items.summary: Stored visual evidence can remain unchanged while its relevance to a current request changes with interaction state. To study this state-dependent source relevance, we introduce SCVIB, a controlled diagnostic benchmark for editable state-conditioned visual instance binding. SCVIB contains 1,050 manually verified support-query pairs and 1,500 multi-turn episodes across five visual domains and four target-state dependencies. Executable state semantics separate target resolution from evidence selection and query-side localization. Direct Qwen3-VL-8B inference achieves 99.53% target-resolution accuracy but 62.00% Joint@0.5, revealing a 37.53-point resolution-localization gap; 563 of its 570 joint failures follow correct target identification. Routing comparisons and fixed-checkpoint support interventions diagnose a post-resolution evidence-utilization bottleneck: successful resolution must be coupled with relevant visual evidence and effective query-side grounding. We introduce TT-VG (Transition-Trace Visual Grounding), a state-conditioned visual grounding framework with an explicit and auditable state-to-evidence-to-grounding path. Target-State Transition Trace (TSTT) executes editable state and selects an auditable support record; Visual Evidence Grounding Adaptation (VEGA) learns support-conditioned grounding from target appearance, boxed support context, and the query. The canonical TT-VG configuration reaches 69.80% Joint@0.5, improving over direct inference by 7.80 points at the combined evidence-utilization and grounding interface. Task adaptation improves the DINOv2 and MASA retrieval baselines to 51.47% and 55.67%, respectively, but both remain substantially below VEGA. These findings highlight state-dependent source selection and evidence utilization as consequential interfaces for interactive multimodal information fusion.
evidence_items.title: SCVIB: Editable State-Conditioned Visual Instance Binding for Multi-Turn Personalized Localization

evidence_items.summary: Optical microscopy lets us watch living bacteria in real time without stains or labels, and it remains the standard instrument for identifying species across clinical, environmental and industrial microbiology. Yet real samples rarely hold a single species. They arrive as mixtures and sometimes carry an organism no model has ever seen. What happens when a model trained on familiar mixtures meets one it has never encountered? No benchmark has asked this of phase-contrast images, so we built one. \textbf{PHOEBI} brings together 120,000 phase-contrast images of 40 mixtures of six bacterial species that we cultured and imaged ourselves, and it holds whole mixtures out of training so that every test is a combination the model has never seen. The answer is sobering. Classifiers that are nearly perfect on the mixtures they know collapse on new ones, and no choice of backbone or pretraining rescues them. The features turn out to be sound and the failure lies in how the evidence within each image is pooled. A culture looks the same everywhere, and decoders built on this simple fact hold steady where large networks fail even though one of them is never trained by gradient descent. The same features go further still. They notice when a species outside the catalogue appears, and the simplest way of giving it a class of its own proves the most effective while leaving the known species almost untouched. PHOEBI turns the mixed culture, the everyday case at the bench, into a measurable target for open-world recognition.
evidence_items.title: PHOEBI: An Open-World Benchmark for Multi-Label Bacterial Identification in Phase-Contrast Microscopy

evidence_items.summary: Step-by-step painting tutorials are used for learning artistic techniques, but existing video resources lack interactivity and personalization. While recent generative models have advanced artistic image synthesis, they still struggle to generate temporally and structurally consistent videos. Video models excel in consistent frame generation, yet fine-tuning an image-to-video model on forward painting sequences creates a long-range dependency on the first-frame reference, disrupting its pretrained attention pattern and hindering reconstruction. We address this issue by training on reversed sequences that better preserve the reference-attention behavior. Building on this, we present Loomis Painter, a framework for reconstructing coherent painting processes. We further introduce a media-transfer training strategy that decouples input appearance from the target process, enabling generation across different artistic media. Trained on a curated dataset of real-world painting processes, our method outperforms existing baselines across LPIPS, DINO, and CLIP metrics and is consistently preferred in expert and non-expert user studies. Code available at https://github.com/Markus-Pobitzer/wlp.
evidence_items.title: Loomis Painter: Learning Painting Processes by Reversing Image-to-Video Generation

METASURFACE-GUIDED MICROROBOTIC CONTROL AT THE LIMIT STARLI | Institute XXIV | Flagship 14 of 30 | Research Group B This prospective research monograph asks when phase-gradient metasurfaces can become reliable optical-control infrastructure for microscopic agents rather than merely generating visually persuasive multifocal wavefronts. Its central research coupling combines metasurface phase-gradient engineering, independently verified optical-field and force shaping, and robust multi-agent positioning under realistic manufacturing, polarization, thermal and task constraints. The investigation follows a falsifiable route from vector electromagnetic interface models and fabricated nanoantenna tolerances to calibrated force and thermofluid attribution, Brownian particle motion, multi-agent collision risk, optical tracking, safe control fallback and cross-batch replication. Ghost foci and polarization drift are treated as testable safety hazards. The strongest conventional benchmarks are optimized spatial light modulators and matched microlens arrays evaluated at equal delivered optical dose, throughput, tracking quality and thermal limits. A metasurface is judged by independently confirmed task completion, not by diffraction efficiency or wavefront quality alone. The manuscript is structured as 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 research chapters with five separately paginated sections each, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. External DOI literature, a four-monograph intellectual lineage and a companion Excel evidence atlas support traceable source navigation and successor-led experiments. The monograph retains negative-result routes: if classical optics provide equal control with lower total risk or cost, that is a meaningful scientific conclusion. The work does not assert a verified autonomous microrobot, a demonstrated multi-agent industrial controller, or a discovered physical law. It is a research architecture that proposes mechanisms, prospective tests, alternative explanations, independent measurements and stopping criteria. Literature from atom trapping, integrated phased arrays and optical force inverse design is explicitly treated as contextual evidence rather than a demonstration of fluidic microrobot autonomy.
